And *la* is negating, meaning: He set the balance so that you do not transgress. It was also said it is *mufassira* (explanatory), because in "setting" there is the sense of "saying." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice, and whoever says the balance is the instrument by which one weighs says its transgression is cheating.

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ (55:9): that is, do not diminish it. He, glory be to Him, first commanded equality, then forbade transgression, which is exceeding the limit by excess, then forbade deficiency, which is loss and cheating.

The majority read *tukhsiru* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *sin*, from *akhsara*. Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and the *sin*, from *khasira*. Both are dialects: it is said *akhsartu al-mizan* and *khasartuhu* (I made the balance deficient).

Then, after He mentioned that He raised the heaven, He mentioned that He set the earth, so He said: ﴿And the earth He set down for the creatures﴾ (55:10), that is, He spread it upon the water for all creation that has life and spirit. There is no basis for restricting *al-anam* (the creatures) to humans and jinn.

The majority read *al-ard* in the accusative by *al-ishtighal*, and Abu al-Simak read it in the nominative by *al-ibtida'*.

The clause ﴿therein is fruit﴾ is in the place of an accusative, as a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of "the earth" implied, and it was said it is a resumptive clause confirming the content of the clause before it. The intended meaning is everything of which one may partake, of all kinds of fruits.

Then, glory be to Him, He singled out the palm for mention because of its nobility and its greater benefit over the rest of the fruits, so He said: ﴿And the palm with its sheaths﴾ (55:11). *Al-akmam* is the plural of *kimm* with a *kasra*, which is the container of dates.

al-Jawhari said: *al-kimm* with a *kasra*, and *al-kimama*, is the container of the spathe (the sheath of the flower cluster), and the cover of an oven. The plural is *kimam*, *akimma*, and *akmam*.

al-Hasan said: "Possessing sheaths" means possessing fiber, because the palm tree is covered with fiber, and its covering (*kimam*) is its fiber. Ibn Zayd said: possessing the spathe before it splits open.

'Ikrima said: possessing husks (*ahmal*).

﴿And the grain, with its husk and the sweet-scented plant﴾ (55:12): *al-habb* is all that is eaten of grains. *Al-'asf*: al-Suddi and al-Farra' said it is the green shoots of the crop, which is the first thing that sprouts from it.

Ibn Kaysan said: It first appears as a leaf, which is *al-'asf*, then a stalk appears for it, then Allah produces sheaths in it, then in the sheaths He produces the grain.

al-Farra' said: The Arabs say, "We went out to *na'sifu* the crop," when they cut from it before it ripened. Likewise he said in *al-Sihah*.

al-Hasan said: *al-'asf* is chaff. Mujahid said: it is the leaves of the tree and the crop.

It was said it is the green leaves of the crop when its head has been cut and it has dried, and from this is His saying: ﴿like a devoured husk﴾ (105:5). It was said it is abundant crop, as one says *qad a'safa al-zar'u* (the crop has become abundant), and *makan mu'sif* (a place abundant in crop). From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:
"When Jumada withholds its rain,
my gardens are adorned by a fertile, crop-rich (*mu'sif*) pasture."

*Al-rayhan* is, according to most, the leafage.

al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said it is the sweet-smelling basil (*rayhan* that is smelled).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands on a stalk.

al-Kalbi said: *al-'asf* is the leaf that is not eaten, and *al-rayhan* is the edible grain.

al-Farra' also said: *al-'asf* is what is eaten of the crop, and *al-rayhan* is what is not eaten. It was said *al-rayhan* is every fragrant-smelling herb.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: One says *shay' rayhani* and *ruhani*, meaning it has a spirit. In *al-Sihah* it is said: *al-rayhan* is a well-known plant, and *al-rayhan* is provision. One says: "I went out seeking Allah's *rayhan*."

al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His *rayhan*,
and His mercy, and a heaven that pours down."

It was said *al-'asf* is the provision of beasts, and *al-rayhan* is the provision of people.

The majority read *wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhanu* with the three in the nominative, coordinated with "fruit." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, and al-Mughira read them in the accusative, coordinated with "the earth," or by an implied verb: meaning "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet-scented plant." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wal-rayhani* in the genitive, coordinated with *al-'asf*.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:13): The address is to the jinn and humans, because the word *al-anam* includes them and others, and then this address is specified to those who understand. The majority of exegetes said this, and what supports it is His saying later: ﴿We shall soon attend to you, O two worlds (*al-thaqalan*)﴾ (55:31). What supports this is what we previously mentioned at the opening of this surah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to the jinn and humans.

It was also said the address is to humans, and it is in the dual by the rule of the Arabs in addressing one person with the dual form, as we previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Cast, both of you, into Gehenna﴾ (50:24).

*Al-ala'* (favors) are blessings.

al-Qurtubi said: This is the saying of all the exegetes. Its singular is *ila* (also *ilan*), like *mi'an* and *'asan*.

Ibn Zayd said: They are power, meaning: "So by which power of your Lord would you deny?" Al-Kalbi also said this.

Allah, glory be to Him, repeated this verse in this surah to affirm the favor and to emphasize the reminder of it, following the custom of the Arabs in expansive speech.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 1–25 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Qutaybi said: God enumerated His bounties in this surah and reminded His creation of His favours. Then He followed every blessing He mentioned with this verse, making it a separator between each pair of blessings, in order to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them. This is like when you say to someone whose kindness to you has been continuous while he denies it: "Were you not poor, and did I not make you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure, and did I not honour you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot, and did I not carry you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a case, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"Do not kill a man, if you are a Muslim woman;*
*Beware of his blood, beware, beware."*

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Repetition drives away heedlessness and reinforces the proof.

﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾. When He, glorified be He, mentioned the creation of the greater world, which is the heavens and the earth and what is in them, He mentioned the creation of the lesser world. By "man" here is meant Adam.

Al-Qurtubi said: This is by agreement among the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil). It is not far-fetched that the intended meaning is the human species, since the children of Adam are created within the creation of their father Adam. *Salsal* (dry clay) is dry clay that produces a ringing sound. It is said it is clay mixed with sand. It is also said it is foul-smelling clay; one says *salla al-lahm* and *asalla* when meat has become foul. Its explanation has already passed in surah al-Hijr. *Fakhkhar* is pottery that has been baked by fire. The meaning is that He created man from clay that resembles pottery in its dryness.

﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾. This means He created the father of the jinn, or the species of jinn, from *marij* of fire. *Marij* is the pure flame of fire. It is said it is its pure part. It is said it is its tongue that appears at its edge when it blazes. Al-Layth said: *al-marij* is a blazing, piercing flame with intense fire.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-marij* is fire let loose that is not restrained. Abu Ubayda said: *al-marij* is a mixture of fire, from *maraja*, meaning to be mixed and agitated.

Al-Jawhari said: "A smokeless flame of fire" is fire that has no smoke, from which the jinn were created.

So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny? For He has bestowed upon you, within the details of your creation and the creation of the jinn, blessings that cannot be counted.

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾. Most readers read *Rabb* with a *raf'* (nominative), as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, He is the Lord of the two easts and the two wests. It is said it is the subject, and its predicate is *maraja al-bahrayn* ("He let loose the two seas"), with what lies between them being a parenthetical clause. The first is preferable. The "two easts" refers to the sunrise of winter and summer, and the "two wests" to their sunsets.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For in that there are blessings that cannot be counted and cannot be easily attained. For one who is fair to himself, denying even one of them is impossible.

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾. *Al-marj* is to leave free and to release. It is said: "I let loose the beast" (*marajtu al-dabba*), when I released it. Its origin is neglect, as a beast grazes freely in pasture. The meaning is that He released each of the two.

*Yaltaqiyan* means they are adjacent, with no separation between them visible to the eye, yet they do not mix. For this reason He said: "Between them is a barrier," that is, a partition that holds them apart, "they do not transgress," meaning neither of them transgresses upon the other by entering into it and mixing with it.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: They are the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome.

Ibn Jurayj said: They are the salty sea and the sweet rivers. It is also said they are the sea of the east and the sea of the west, and it is said they are the sea of pearls and coral, and it is said they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They meet every year. It is also said their two edges meet.

His saying *yaltaqiyan* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to *al-bahrayn*. The clause "between them is a barrier" may be a new independent sentence, or it may be a circumstantial clause.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For this verse and others like it cannot be denied in any way.

﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾.
The majority read *yakhruju* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *ra'*, in the active voice. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ra'*, in the passive voice. *Al-lu'lu'* is pearl, and *al-marjan* is the well-known red beads.

Al-Farra' said: *al-lu'lu'* are the large ones, and *al-marjan* are the small ones.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the view of all the lexicographers (ahl al-lugha).

Muqatil, al-Suddi and Mujahid said: *al-lu'lu'* are its small ones and *al-marjan* its large ones. And He said "from them," though these come forth only from the salty sea and not from the sweet one; for if it comes out of one of them, it has come out of both. So said al-Zajjaj and others.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: This is an instance of omitting a modifier: the meaning is "from one of them," as in His saying: "upon a great man from the two towns" (al-Zukhruf 31).

Al-Akhfash said: A group claims that pearls come forth from the sweet water. It is also said that they are two seas, from one of which the pearls come forth and from the other the coral. It is also said they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth: when rainwater falls into the shell of the sea, it solidifies into a pearl, and thus it comes forth from both.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For in that there are signs that no one can deny or refuse to acknowledge.

﴿And His are the ships that sail in the sea like mountains﴾. By *al-jawari* is meant the ships running in the sea. *Al-munsha'at* are the raised ones, whose wood has been lifted up upon one another and assembled until they rise high and grow long, until they become in the sea like landmarks (*a'lam*), which are mountains. *Al-'alam* is a tall mountain.

Qatada said: *al-munsha'at* are the created things for running.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-munsha'at* are the ones made to run. The explanation of this has already passed in surah al-Shura.

The majority read *al-jawari* with a *kasra* on the *ra'* and the *ya'* elided because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Amr in one transmission from him read it with a *damma* on the *ra'*, disregarding the elision. Ya'qub read it with the *ya'* retained. The majority read *al-munsha'at* with a *fatha* on the *shin*; Hamza and Abu Bakr in one transmission from him read it with a *kasra* on the *shin*.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For that is so clear and manifest that its denial or refusal is impossible.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾, that he said: "By calculation and by stations through which they travel."

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning ﴿And the earth He laid out for all creatures﴾, that he said: "For the people."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, that he said: "For the creation."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "Everything that has a soul."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿And the palm tree with its sheaths﴾, that he said: "The containers of the spathe."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾, that he said: "The husk (*tibn*)." And "the fragrant plants" (*al-rayhan*), he said: "The greenness of the crops."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "*Al-'asf*" is the leaves of the crop when they dry out, and "*al-rayhan*" is what the earth produces of the fragrant plants that are smelled.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, that he said: "*Al-'asf*" is the crop when it first emerges as green shoots, and "*al-rayhan*" is when it stands firm on its stalk and has not yet formed an ear.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "Every *rayhan* in the Qur'an is provision (*rizq*)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾, that he said: "That is, which of God's blessings."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "That is, the jinn and the humans."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also concerning ﴿from a smokeless flame of fire﴾, that he said: "From the flame of fire."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "The pure part of the fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾, that he said: "The sun has a rising point in winter and a setting point in winter, and a rising point in summer and a setting point in summer, different from its rising point in winter and its setting point in winter."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning the verse, that he said: "The rising of the dawn and the rising of the twilight, and the setting of the sun and the setting of the twilight."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾, that he said: "He released the two seas. ﴿Between them is a barrier﴾," he said: "A partition. ﴿They do not transgress﴾, they do not mix."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "The sea of the sky and the sea of the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿Between them is a barrier, they do not transgress﴾, that he said: "Between them is such a distance that neither one transgresses upon the other."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾, that he said: "When the sky rains, the shells in the sea open their mouths, and whatever falls into them of the raindrops of the sky becomes pearl."

(p-1436) 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he said: "Coral is the large pearls."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Pearl is what is large of it, and coral is the small pearls."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "Coral is red beads."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 55, verses 1–25 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.

Al-Qurtubi said: The whole surah is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata', and Jabir. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Except for one verse within it, which is His saying: ﴿He is asked by whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ (55:29)."

Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said it is entirely Medinan. The first view is more sound, and it is supported by what al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'isha, who said: "The surah ﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾ (55:1–2) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a *hasan* (good) chain, from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting while praying toward the Corner (of the Ka'ba), before he was commanded to proclaim openly, and the polytheists were listening: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:13)."

The second view is supported by what Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Medina." The two views can be reconciled by saying that part of it was revealed in Mecca and part in Medina.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from its beginning to its end, and they remained silent. He said: 'Why do I see you silent? I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they gave a better response than you did. Every time I reached His saying: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾, they said: "None of Your blessings do we deny, our Lord, and to You belongs all praise."'"

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: "This is a *gharib* (strange) hadith, which we do not know except through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad." [p. 1433]

It is related from Imam Ahmad that he used to disapprove of his narrating from Zuhayr.

al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it to be narrated except by this route."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib in his *Tarikh* narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and al-Suyuti declared its chain sound.

al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it to be narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) except by this route with this chain."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from 'Ali, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Everything has a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is al-Rahman.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾: The *raf'* (nominative case) of "al-Rahman" is because it is the *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and what follows it of verbs are its *akhbar* (predicates).

It may also be that it is the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'*, meaning: "He is Allah, the Most Merciful."

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ is "made it easy."

al-Kalbi said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ to Muhammad, and Muhammad taught it to his community. It was also said that He made it a sign of what He has made people worship by. It was said that this verse was revealed as a response to the people of Mecca when they said: "It is only a human who teaches him." It was also said it was a response to their saying: "And what is al-Rahman?"

Since this surah enumerates the favors which He has bestowed upon His servants, He began with the favor that is greatest in rank, most abundant in benefit, most complete in usefulness, and most far-reaching in its return, which is the favor of teaching the Qur'an, for it is the axis of the happiness of both abodes, the pivot of both goods, and the pillar of both matters.

Then, after this favor, He bestowed the favor of creation, which is the basis of all affairs and the return of all things, and so He said: ﴿He created man﴾ (55:3). Thirdly, He bestowed favor by teaching him *al-bayan* (clear expression), by which understanding occurs, on which mutual discourse turns, and upon which the interests of this life and the Hereafter depend, for it is impossible to make manifest what is in the hearts or to reveal what turns in the mind except by it.

Qatada and al-Hasan said: "The intended 'man' here is Muhammad (ﷺ), and by *al-bayan* is meant the lawful from the unlawful and guidance from misguidance." But this is far-fetched.

al-Dahhak said: *al-bayan* is good and evil.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is what benefits him from what harms him.

It was said: *al-bayan* is writing with the pen.

The better view is to take "man" as the species, and to take *al-bayan* as Allah teaching every people their language, which they speak.

﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning﴾ (55:5): That is, they run according to calculation and to stations which they do not exceed, and by this they indicate the number of months and years.

Qatada and Abu Malik said: They run by a reckoning in their stations; they do not exceed them nor deviate from them.

Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kaysan said: It means that by them times, terms, and deeds are reckoned.

Had there been no night and day, the sun and the moon, no one would know how to calculate, because the age would be entirely night or entirely day.

al-Dahhak said: The meaning of *bi-husban* is "by measure."

Mujahid said: *bi-husban* is like the *husban* of a millstone, meaning its axis upon which they both revolve.

al-Akhfash said: *al-husban* is the plural of *al-hisab* (reckoning), like *shuhub* and *shuhban*.

As for *al-husban* with a *damma*, it means punishment, as has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ (55:6): *al-najm* is the plant that has no stalk, and *al-shajar* is that which has a stalk.

The poet said:
"The wide plain has grown its thickets of low plants,
and by it the two tribes of Tamim and Wa'il have been completed."

And Zuhayr said:
"Crowned with the roots of the *najm*, which the south wind weaves
for the bright waters of its surface, its patterns."

The intended meaning of their prostration is their submission to Allah, Exalted, in the manner of the prostrating among the responsible beings.

al-Farra' said: Their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then incline with it when the shade recedes.

al-Zajjaj said: Their prostration is the turning of the shadow with them, as in His saying: ﴿whose shadows turn around﴾ (16:48).

al-Hasan and Mujahid said: The intended "star" is a star of the sky, and its prostration is its rising. Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

It was also said: its prostration is its setting. And the prostration of the tree is its allowing its fruit to be picked.

al-Nahhas said: The origin of *sujud* (prostration) is submission and compliance to Allah. This sentence and the one before it are two other predicates of *al-Rahman*, and the connecting pronoun is omitted in them because it is clear, as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him."

﴿And the heaven He raised﴾ (55:7): The majority read *al-sama'* in the accusative by *al-ishtighal* (the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun, so the noun is put in the accusative).

Abu al-Simak read it in the nominative by *al-ibtida'* (inception of a nominal sentence). The meaning is that He made the heaven raised above the earth. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾: The intended "balance" is justice. That is: He set in the earth the justice which He commanded. Thus said Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that He commanded us to do justice, and what indicates this is His saying: ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ (55:8), that is, do not exceed justice.

al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: The intended meaning is the instrument of weighing, by which one reaches fairness and equity.

It was said the balance is the Qur'an, because in it is the explanation of what is needed. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said this, but the first view is better.

Then, after informing the servants that He had set it for them, He commanded them to establish justice, so He said: ﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾ (55:9), that is, make your weighing upright with justice. It was also said the meaning is: establish the tongue of the balance with justice. It was also said the meaning is: He set the balance for the weighing of deeds in the Hereafter.

In His saying ﴿that you not transgress﴾, *an* is *masdariyya* (a verbal-noun particle), meaning "so that you do not transgress." And *la* is negating, meaning: He set the balance so that you do not transgress. It was also said it is *mufassira* (explanatory), because in "setting" there is the sense of "saying." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice, and whoever says the balance is the instrument by which one weighs says its transgression is cheating.

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ (55:9): that is, do not diminish it. He, glory be to Him, first commanded equality, then forbade transgression, which is exceeding the limit by excess, then forbade deficiency, which is loss and cheating.

The majority read *tukhsiru* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *sin*, from *akhsara*. Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and the *sin*, from *khasira*. Both are dialects: it is said *akhsartu al-mizan* and *khasartuhu* (I made the balance deficient).

Then, after He mentioned that He raised the heaven, He mentioned that He set the earth, so He said: ﴿And the earth He set down for the creatures﴾ (55:10), that is, He spread it upon the water for all creation that has life and spirit. There is no basis for restricting *al-anam* (the creatures) to humans and jinn.

The majority read *al-ard* in the accusative by *al-ishtighal*, and Abu al-Simak read it in the nominative by *al-ibtida'*.

The clause ﴿therein is fruit﴾ is in the place of an accusative, as a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of "the earth" implied, and it was said it is a resumptive clause confirming the content of the clause before it. The intended meaning is everything of which one may partake, of all kinds of fruits.

Then, glory be to Him, He singled out the palm for mention because of its nobility and its greater benefit over the rest of the fruits, so He said: ﴿And the palm with its sheaths﴾ (55:11). *Al-akmam* is the plural of *kimm* with a *kasra*, which is the container of dates.

al-Jawhari said: *al-kimm* with a *kasra*, and *al-kimama*, is the container of the spathe (the sheath of the flower cluster), and the cover of an oven. The plural is *kimam*, *akimma*, and *akmam*.

al-Hasan said: "Possessing sheaths" means possessing fiber, because the palm tree is covered with fiber, and its covering (*kimam*) is its fiber. Ibn Zayd said: possessing the spathe before it splits open.

'Ikrima said: possessing husks (*ahmal*).

﴿And the grain, with its husk and the sweet-scented plant﴾ (55:12): *al-habb* is all that is eaten of grains. *Al-'asf*: al-Suddi and al-Farra' said it is the green shoots of the crop, which is the first thing that sprouts from it.

Ibn Kaysan said: It first appears as a leaf, which is *al-'asf*, then a stalk appears for it, then Allah produces sheaths in it, then in the sheaths He produces the grain.

al-Farra' said: The Arabs say, "We went out to *na'sifu* the crop," when they cut from it before it ripened. Likewise he said in *al-Sihah*.

al-Hasan said: *al-'asf* is chaff. Mujahid said: it is the leaves of the tree and the crop.

It was said it is the green leaves of the crop when its head has been cut and it has dried, and from this is His saying: ﴿like a devoured husk﴾ (105:5). It was said it is abundant crop, as one says *qad a'safa al-zar'u* (the crop has become abundant), and *makan mu'sif* (a place abundant in crop). From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:
"When Jumada withholds its rain,
my gardens are adorned by a fertile, crop-rich (*mu'sif*) pasture."

*Al-rayhan* is, according to most, the leafage.

al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said it is the sweet-smelling basil (*rayhan* that is smelled).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands on a stalk.

al-Kalbi said: *al-'asf* is the leaf that is not eaten, and *al-rayhan* is the edible grain.

al-Farra' also said: *al-'asf* is what is eaten of the crop, and *al-rayhan* is what is not eaten. It was said *al-rayhan* is every fragrant-smelling herb.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: One says *shay' rayhani* and *ruhani*, meaning it has a spirit. In *al-Sihah* it is said: *al-rayhan* is a well-known plant, and *al-rayhan* is provision. One says: "I went out seeking Allah's *rayhan*."

al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His *rayhan*,
and His mercy, and a heaven that pours down."

It was said *al-'asf* is the provision of beasts, and *al-rayhan* is the provision of people.

The majority read *wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhanu* with the three in the nominative, coordinated with "fruit." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, and al-Mughira read them in the accusative, coordinated with "the earth," or by an implied verb: meaning "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet-scented plant." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wal-rayhani* in the genitive, coordinated with *al-'asf*.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:13): The address is to the jinn and humans, because the word *al-anam* includes them and others, and then this address is specified to those who understand. The majority of exegetes said this, and what supports it is His saying later: ﴿We shall soon attend to you, O two worlds (*al-thaqalan*)﴾ (55:31). What supports this is what we previously mentioned at the opening of this surah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to the jinn and humans.

It was also said the address is to humans, and it is in the dual by the rule of the Arabs in addressing one person with the dual form, as we previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Cast, both of you, into Gehenna﴾ (50:24).

*Al-ala'* (favors) are blessings.

al-Qurtubi said: This is the saying of all the exegetes. Its singular is *ila* (also *ilan*), like *mi'an* and *'asan*.

Ibn Zayd said: They are power, meaning: "So by which power of your Lord would you deny?" Al-Kalbi also said this.

Allah, glory be to Him, repeated this verse in this surah to affirm the favor and to emphasize the reminder of it, following the custom of the Arabs in expansive speech.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 1–25 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Qutaybi said: God enumerated His bounties in this surah and reminded His creation of His favours. Then He followed every blessing He mentioned with this verse, making it a separator between each pair of blessings, in order to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them. This is like when you say to someone whose kindness to you has been continuous while he denies it: "Were you not poor, and did I not make you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure, and did I not honour you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot, and did I not carry you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a case, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"Do not kill a man, if you are a Muslim woman;*
*Beware of his blood, beware, beware."*

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Repetition drives away heedlessness and reinforces the proof.

﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾. When He, glorified be He, mentioned the creation of the greater world, which is the heavens and the earth and what is in them, He mentioned the creation of the lesser world. By "man" here is meant Adam.

Al-Qurtubi said: This is by agreement among the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil). It is not far-fetched that the intended meaning is the human species, since the children of Adam are created within the creation of their father Adam. *Salsal* (dry clay) is dry clay that produces a ringing sound. It is said it is clay mixed with sand. It is also said it is foul-smelling clay; one says *salla al-lahm* and *asalla* when meat has become foul. Its explanation has already passed in surah al-Hijr. *Fakhkhar* is pottery that has been baked by fire. The meaning is that He created man from clay that resembles pottery in its dryness.

﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾. This means He created the father of the jinn, or the species of jinn, from *marij* of fire. *Marij* is the pure flame of fire. It is said it is its pure part. It is said it is its tongue that appears at its edge when it blazes. Al-Layth said: *al-marij* is a blazing, piercing flame with intense fire.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-marij* is fire let loose that is not restrained. Abu Ubayda said: *al-marij* is a mixture of fire, from *maraja*, meaning to be mixed and agitated.

Al-Jawhari said: "A smokeless flame of fire" is fire that has no smoke, from which the jinn were created.

So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny? For He has bestowed upon you, within the details of your creation and the creation of the jinn, blessings that cannot be counted.

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾. Most readers read *Rabb* with a *raf'* (nominative), as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, He is the Lord of the two easts and the two wests. It is said it is the subject, and its predicate is *maraja al-bahrayn* ("He let loose the two seas"), with what lies between them being a parenthetical clause. The first is preferable. The "two easts" refers to the sunrise of winter and summer, and the "two wests" to their sunsets.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For in that there are blessings that cannot be counted and cannot be easily attained. For one who is fair to himself, denying even one of them is impossible.

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾. *Al-marj* is to leave free and to release. It is said: "I let loose the beast" (*marajtu al-dabba*), when I released it. Its origin is neglect, as a beast grazes freely in pasture. The meaning is that He released each of the two.

*Yaltaqiyan* means they are adjacent, with no separation between them visible to the eye, yet they do not mix. For this reason He said: "Between them is a barrier," that is, a partition that holds them apart, "they do not transgress," meaning neither of them transgresses upon the other by entering into it and mixing with it.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: They are the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome.

Ibn Jurayj said: They are the salty sea and the sweet rivers. It is also said they are the sea of the east and the sea of the west, and it is said they are the sea of pearls and coral, and it is said they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They meet every year. It is also said their two edges meet.

His saying *yaltaqiyan* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to *al-bahrayn*. The clause "between them is a barrier" may be a new independent sentence, or it may be a circumstantial clause.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For this verse and others like it cannot be denied in any way.

﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾.
The majority read *yakhruju* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *ra'*, in the active voice. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ra'*, in the passive voice. *Al-lu'lu'* is pearl, and *al-marjan* is the well-known red beads.

Al-Farra' said: *al-lu'lu'* are the large ones, and *al-marjan* are the small ones.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the view of all the lexicographers (ahl al-lugha).

Muqatil, al-Suddi and Mujahid said: *al-lu'lu'* are its small ones and *al-marjan* its large ones. And He said "from them," though these come forth only from the salty sea and not from the sweet one; for if it comes out of one of them, it has come out of both. So said al-Zajjaj and others.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: This is an instance of omitting a modifier: the meaning is "from one of them," as in His saying: "upon a great man from the two towns" (al-Zukhruf 31).

Al-Akhfash said: A group claims that pearls come forth from the sweet water. It is also said that they are two seas, from one of which the pearls come forth and from the other the coral. It is also said they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth: when rainwater falls into the shell of the sea, it solidifies into a pearl, and thus it comes forth from both.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For in that there are signs that no one can deny or refuse to acknowledge.

﴿And His are the ships that sail in the sea like mountains﴾. By *al-jawari* is meant the ships running in the sea. *Al-munsha'at* are the raised ones, whose wood has been lifted up upon one another and assembled until they rise high and grow long, until they become in the sea like landmarks (*a'lam*), which are mountains. *Al-'alam* is a tall mountain.

Qatada said: *al-munsha'at* are the created things for running.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-munsha'at* are the ones made to run. The explanation of this has already passed in surah al-Shura.

The majority read *al-jawari* with a *kasra* on the *ra'* and the *ya'* elided because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Amr in one transmission from him read it with a *damma* on the *ra'*, disregarding the elision. Ya'qub read it with the *ya'* retained. The majority read *al-munsha'at* with a *fatha* on the *shin*; Hamza and Abu Bakr in one transmission from him read it with a *kasra* on the *shin*.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For that is so clear and manifest that its denial or refusal is impossible.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾, that he said: "By calculation and by stations through which they travel."

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning ﴿And the earth He laid out for all creatures﴾, that he said: "For the people."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, that he said: "For the creation."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "Everything that has a soul."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿And the palm tree with its sheaths﴾, that he said: "The containers of the spathe."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾, that he said: "The husk (*tibn*)." And "the fragrant plants" (*al-rayhan*), he said: "The greenness of the crops."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "*Al-'asf*" is the leaves of the crop when they dry out, and "*al-rayhan*" is what the earth produces of the fragrant plants that are smelled.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, that he said: "*Al-'asf*" is the crop when it first emerges as green shoots, and "*al-rayhan*" is when it stands firm on its stalk and has not yet formed an ear.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "Every *rayhan* in the Qur'an is provision (*rizq*)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾, that he said: "That is, which of God's blessings."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "That is, the jinn and the humans."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also concerning ﴿from a smokeless flame of fire﴾, that he said: "From the flame of fire."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "The pure part of the fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾, that he said: "The sun has a rising point in winter and a setting point in winter, and a rising point in summer and a setting point in summer, different from its rising point in winter and its setting point in winter."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning the verse, that he said: "The rising of the dawn and the rising of the twilight, and the setting of the sun and the setting of the twilight."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾, that he said: "He released the two seas. ﴿Between them is a barrier﴾," he said: "A partition. ﴿They do not transgress﴾, they do not mix."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "The sea of the sky and the sea of the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿Between them is a barrier, they do not transgress﴾, that he said: "Between them is such a distance that neither one transgresses upon the other."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾, that he said: "When the sky rains, the shells in the sea open their mouths, and whatever falls into them of the raindrops of the sky becomes pearl."

(p-1436) 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he said: "Coral is the large pearls."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Pearl is what is large of it, and coral is the small pearls."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "Coral is red beads."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 55, verses 1–25 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.

Al-Qurtubi said: The whole surah is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata', and Jabir. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Except for one verse within it, which is His saying: ﴿He is asked by whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ (55:29)."

Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said it is entirely Medinan. The first view is more sound, and it is supported by what al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'isha, who said: "The surah ﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾ (55:1–2) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a *hasan* (good) chain, from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting while praying toward the Corner (of the Ka'ba), before he was commanded to proclaim openly, and the polytheists were listening: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:13)."

The second view is supported by what Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Medina." The two views can be reconciled by saying that part of it was revealed in Mecca and part in Medina.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from its beginning to its end, and they remained silent. He said: 'Why do I see you silent? I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they gave a better response than you did. Every time I reached His saying: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾, they said: "None of Your blessings do we deny, our Lord, and to You belongs all praise."'"

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: "This is a *gharib* (strange) hadith, which we do not know except through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad." [p. 1433]

It is related from Imam Ahmad that he used to disapprove of his narrating from Zuhayr.

al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it to be narrated except by this route."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib in his *Tarikh* narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and al-Suyuti declared its chain sound.

al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it to be narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) except by this route with this chain."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from 'Ali, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Everything has a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is al-Rahman.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾: The *raf'* (nominative case) of "al-Rahman" is because it is the *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and what follows it of verbs are its *akhbar* (predicates).

It may also be that it is the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'*, meaning: "He is Allah, the Most Merciful."

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ is "made it easy."

al-Kalbi said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ to Muhammad, and Muhammad taught it to his community. It was also said that He made it a sign of what He has made people worship by. It was said that this verse was revealed as a response to the people of Mecca when they said: "It is only a human who teaches him." It was also said it was a response to their saying: "And what is al-Rahman?"

Since this surah enumerates the favors which He has bestowed upon His servants, He began with the favor that is greatest in rank, most abundant in benefit, most complete in usefulness, and most far-reaching in its return, which is the favor of teaching the Qur'an, for it is the axis of the happiness of both abodes, the pivot of both goods, and the pillar of both matters.

Then, after this favor, He bestowed the favor of creation, which is the basis of all affairs and the return of all things, and so He said: ﴿He created man﴾ (55:3). Thirdly, He bestowed favor by teaching him *al-bayan* (clear expression), by which understanding occurs, on which mutual discourse turns, and upon which the interests of this life and the Hereafter depend, for it is impossible to make manifest what is in the hearts or to reveal what turns in the mind except by it.

Qatada and al-Hasan said: "The intended 'man' here is Muhammad (ﷺ), and by *al-bayan* is meant the lawful from the unlawful and guidance from misguidance." But this is far-fetched.

al-Dahhak said: *al-bayan* is good and evil.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is what benefits him from what harms him.

It was said: *al-bayan* is writing with the pen.

The better view is to take "man" as the species, and to take *al-bayan* as Allah teaching every people their language, which they speak.

﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning﴾ (55:5): That is, they run according to calculation and to stations which they do not exceed, and by this they indicate the number of months and years.

Qatada and Abu Malik said: They run by a reckoning in their stations; they do not exceed them nor deviate from them.

Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kaysan said: It means that by them times, terms, and deeds are reckoned.

Had there been no night and day, the sun and the moon, no one would know how to calculate, because the age would be entirely night or entirely day.

al-Dahhak said: The meaning of *bi-husban* is "by measure."

Mujahid said: *bi-husban* is like the *husban* of a millstone, meaning its axis upon which they both revolve.

al-Akhfash said: *al-husban* is the plural of *al-hisab* (reckoning), like *shuhub* and *shuhban*.

As for *al-husban* with a *damma*, it means punishment, as has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ (55:6): *al-najm* is the plant that has no stalk, and *al-shajar* is that which has a stalk.

The poet said:
"The wide plain has grown its thickets of low plants,
and by it the two tribes of Tamim and Wa'il have been completed."

And Zuhayr said:
"Crowned with the roots of the *najm*, which the south wind weaves
for the bright waters of its surface, its patterns."

The intended meaning of their prostration is their submission to Allah, Exalted, in the manner of the prostrating among the responsible beings.

al-Farra' said: Their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then incline with it when the shade recedes.

al-Zajjaj said: Their prostration is the turning of the shadow with them, as in His saying: ﴿whose shadows turn around﴾ (16:48).

al-Hasan and Mujahid said: The intended "star" is a star of the sky, and its prostration is its rising. Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

It was also said: its prostration is its setting. And the prostration of the tree is its allowing its fruit to be picked.

al-Nahhas said: The origin of *sujud* (prostration) is submission and compliance to Allah. This sentence and the one before it are two other predicates of *al-Rahman*, and the connecting pronoun is omitted in them because it is clear, as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him."

﴿And the heaven He raised﴾ (55:7): The majority read *al-sama'* in the accusative by *al-ishtighal* (the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun, so the noun is put in the accusative).

Abu al-Simak read it in the nominative by *al-ibtida'* (inception of a nominal sentence). The meaning is that He made the heaven raised above the earth. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾: The intended "balance" is justice. That is: He set in the earth the justice which He commanded. Thus said Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that He commanded us to do justice, and what indicates this is His saying: ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ (55:8), that is, do not exceed justice.

al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: The intended meaning is the instrument of weighing, by which one reaches fairness and equity.

It was said the balance is the Qur'an, because in it is the explanation of what is needed. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said this, but the first view is better.

Then, after informing the servants that He had set it for them, He commanded them to establish justice, so He said: ﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾ (55:9), that is, make your weighing upright with justice. It was also said the meaning is: establish the tongue of the balance with justice. It was also said the meaning is: He set the balance for the weighing of deeds in the Hereafter.

In His saying ﴿that you not transgress﴾, *an* is *masdariyya* (a verbal-noun particle), meaning "so that you do not transgress." And *la* is negating, meaning: He set the balance so that you do not transgress. It was also said it is *mufassira* (explanatory), because in "setting" there is the sense of "saying." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice, and whoever says the balance is the instrument by which one weighs says its transgression is cheating.

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ (55:9): that is, do not diminish it. He, glory be to Him, first commanded equality, then forbade transgression, which is exceeding the limit by excess, then forbade deficiency, which is loss and cheating.

The majority read *tukhsiru* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *sin*, from *akhsara*. Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and the *sin*, from *khasira*. Both are dialects: it is said *akhsartu al-mizan* and *khasartuhu* (I made the balance deficient).

Then, after He mentioned that He raised the heaven, He mentioned that He set the earth, so He said: ﴿And the earth He set down for the creatures﴾ (55:10), that is, He spread it upon the water for all creation that has life and spirit. There is no basis for restricting *al-anam* (the creatures) to humans and jinn.

The majority read *al-ard* in the accusative by *al-ishtighal*, and Abu al-Simak read it in the nominative by *al-ibtida'*.

The clause ﴿therein is fruit﴾ is in the place of an accusative, as a *hal* (circumstantial clause) of "the earth" implied, and it was said it is a resumptive clause confirming the content of the clause before it. The intended meaning is everything of which one may partake, of all kinds of fruits.

Then, glory be to Him, He singled out the palm for mention because of its nobility and its greater benefit over the rest of the fruits, so He said: ﴿And the palm with its sheaths﴾ (55:11). *Al-akmam* is the plural of *kimm* with a *kasra*, which is the container of dates.

al-Jawhari said: *al-kimm* with a *kasra*, and *al-kimama*, is the container of the spathe (the sheath of the flower cluster), and the cover of an oven. The plural is *kimam*, *akimma*, and *akmam*.

al-Hasan said: "Possessing sheaths" means possessing fiber, because the palm tree is covered with fiber, and its covering (*kimam*) is its fiber. Ibn Zayd said: possessing the spathe before it splits open.

'Ikrima said: possessing husks (*ahmal*).

﴿And the grain, with its husk and the sweet-scented plant﴾ (55:12): *al-habb* is all that is eaten of grains. *Al-'asf*: al-Suddi and al-Farra' said it is the green shoots of the crop, which is the first thing that sprouts from it.

Ibn Kaysan said: It first appears as a leaf, which is *al-'asf*, then a stalk appears for it, then Allah produces sheaths in it, then in the sheaths He produces the grain.

al-Farra' said: The Arabs say, "We went out to *na'sifu* the crop," when they cut from it before it ripened. Likewise he said in *al-Sihah*.

al-Hasan said: *al-'asf* is chaff. Mujahid said: it is the leaves of the tree and the crop.

It was said it is the green leaves of the crop when its head has been cut and it has dried, and from this is His saying: ﴿like a devoured husk﴾ (105:5). It was said it is abundant crop, as one says *qad a'safa al-zar'u* (the crop has become abundant), and *makan mu'sif* (a place abundant in crop). From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:
"When Jumada withholds its rain,
my gardens are adorned by a fertile, crop-rich (*mu'sif*) pasture."

*Al-rayhan* is, according to most, the leafage.

al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd said it is the sweet-smelling basil (*rayhan* that is smelled).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it is what stands on a stalk.

al-Kalbi said: *al-'asf* is the leaf that is not eaten, and *al-rayhan* is the edible grain.

al-Farra' also said: *al-'asf* is what is eaten of the crop, and *al-rayhan* is what is not eaten. It was said *al-rayhan* is every fragrant-smelling herb.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: One says *shay' rayhani* and *ruhani*, meaning it has a spirit. In *al-Sihah* it is said: *al-rayhan* is a well-known plant, and *al-rayhan* is provision. One says: "I went out seeking Allah's *rayhan*."

al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:
"The peace of God and His *rayhan*,
and His mercy, and a heaven that pours down."

It was said *al-'asf* is the provision of beasts, and *al-rayhan* is the provision of people.

The majority read *wal-habbu dhu al-'asfi wal-rayhanu* with the three in the nominative, coordinated with "fruit." Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, and al-Mughira read them in the accusative, coordinated with "the earth," or by an implied verb: meaning "and He created the grain possessing husk and the sweet-scented plant." Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wal-rayhani* in the genitive, coordinated with *al-'asf*.

﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:13): The address is to the jinn and humans, because the word *al-anam* includes them and others, and then this address is specified to those who understand. The majority of exegetes said this, and what supports it is His saying later: ﴿We shall soon attend to you, O two worlds (*al-thaqalan*)﴾ (55:31). What supports this is what we previously mentioned at the opening of this surah: that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to the jinn and humans.

It was also said the address is to humans, and it is in the dual by the rule of the Arabs in addressing one person with the dual form, as we previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿Cast, both of you, into Gehenna﴾ (50:24).

*Al-ala'* (favors) are blessings.

al-Qurtubi said: This is the saying of all the exegetes. Its singular is *ila* (also *ilan*), like *mi'an* and *'asan*.

Ibn Zayd said: They are power, meaning: "So by which power of your Lord would you deny?" Al-Kalbi also said this.

Allah, glory be to Him, repeated this verse in this surah to affirm the favor and to emphasize the reminder of it, following the custom of the Arabs in expansive speech.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 1–25 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Qutaybi said: God enumerated His bounties in this surah and reminded His creation of His favours. Then He followed every blessing He mentioned with this verse, making it a separator between each pair of blessings, in order to alert them to the blessings and to make them acknowledge them. This is like when you say to someone whose kindness to you has been continuous while he denies it: "Were you not poor, and did I not make you rich? Will you deny this? Were you not obscure, and did I not honour you? Will you deny this? Were you not on foot, and did I not carry you? Will you deny this?" Repetition is good in such a case, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*"Do not kill a man, if you are a Muslim woman;*
*Beware of his blood, beware, beware."*

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: Repetition drives away heedlessness and reinforces the proof.

﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾. When He, glorified be He, mentioned the creation of the greater world, which is the heavens and the earth and what is in them, He mentioned the creation of the lesser world. By "man" here is meant Adam.

Al-Qurtubi said: This is by agreement among the exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil). It is not far-fetched that the intended meaning is the human species, since the children of Adam are created within the creation of their father Adam. *Salsal* (dry clay) is dry clay that produces a ringing sound. It is said it is clay mixed with sand. It is also said it is foul-smelling clay; one says *salla al-lahm* and *asalla* when meat has become foul. Its explanation has already passed in surah al-Hijr. *Fakhkhar* is pottery that has been baked by fire. The meaning is that He created man from clay that resembles pottery in its dryness.

﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾. This means He created the father of the jinn, or the species of jinn, from *marij* of fire. *Marij* is the pure flame of fire. It is said it is its pure part. It is said it is its tongue that appears at its edge when it blazes. Al-Layth said: *al-marij* is a blazing, piercing flame with intense fire.

Al-Mubarrad said: *al-marij* is fire let loose that is not restrained. Abu Ubayda said: *al-marij* is a mixture of fire, from *maraja*, meaning to be mixed and agitated.

Al-Jawhari said: "A smokeless flame of fire" is fire that has no smoke, from which the jinn were created.

So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny? For He has bestowed upon you, within the details of your creation and the creation of the jinn, blessings that cannot be counted.

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾. Most readers read *Rabb* with a *raf'* (nominative), as the predicate of an omitted subject: that is, He is the Lord of the two easts and the two wests. It is said it is the subject, and its predicate is *maraja al-bahrayn* ("He let loose the two seas"), with what lies between them being a parenthetical clause. The first is preferable. The "two easts" refers to the sunrise of winter and summer, and the "two wests" to their sunsets.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For in that there are blessings that cannot be counted and cannot be easily attained. For one who is fair to himself, denying even one of them is impossible.

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾. *Al-marj* is to leave free and to release. It is said: "I let loose the beast" (*marajtu al-dabba*), when I released it. Its origin is neglect, as a beast grazes freely in pasture. The meaning is that He released each of the two.

*Yaltaqiyan* means they are adjacent, with no separation between them visible to the eye, yet they do not mix. For this reason He said: "Between them is a barrier," that is, a partition that holds them apart, "they do not transgress," meaning neither of them transgresses upon the other by entering into it and mixing with it.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: They are the Sea of Persia and the Sea of Rome.

Ibn Jurayj said: They are the salty sea and the sweet rivers. It is also said they are the sea of the east and the sea of the west, and it is said they are the sea of pearls and coral, and it is said they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: They meet every year. It is also said their two edges meet.

His saying *yaltaqiyan* is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to *al-bahrayn*. The clause "between them is a barrier" may be a new independent sentence, or it may be a circumstantial clause.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For this verse and others like it cannot be denied in any way.

﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾.
The majority read *yakhruju* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *ra'*, in the active voice. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read it with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ra'*, in the passive voice. *Al-lu'lu'* is pearl, and *al-marjan* is the well-known red beads.

Al-Farra' said: *al-lu'lu'* are the large ones, and *al-marjan* are the small ones.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the view of all the lexicographers (ahl al-lugha).

Muqatil, al-Suddi and Mujahid said: *al-lu'lu'* are its small ones and *al-marjan* its large ones. And He said "from them," though these come forth only from the salty sea and not from the sweet one; for if it comes out of one of them, it has come out of both. So said al-Zajjaj and others.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: This is an instance of omitting a modifier: the meaning is "from one of them," as in His saying: "upon a great man from the two towns" (al-Zukhruf 31).

Al-Akhfash said: A group claims that pearls come forth from the sweet water. It is also said that they are two seas, from one of which the pearls come forth and from the other the coral. It is also said they are the sea of the sky and the sea of the earth: when rainwater falls into the shell of the sea, it solidifies into a pearl, and thus it comes forth from both.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For in that there are signs that no one can deny or refuse to acknowledge.

﴿And His are the ships that sail in the sea like mountains﴾. By *al-jawari* is meant the ships running in the sea. *Al-munsha'at* are the raised ones, whose wood has been lifted up upon one another and assembled until they rise high and grow long, until they become in the sea like landmarks (*a'lam*), which are mountains. *Al-'alam* is a tall mountain.

Qatada said: *al-munsha'at* are the created things for running.

Al-Akhfash said: *al-munsha'at* are the ones made to run. The explanation of this has already passed in surah al-Shura.

The majority read *al-jawari* with a *kasra* on the *ra'* and the *ya'* elided because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Abu 'Amr in one transmission from him read it with a *damma* on the *ra'*, disregarding the elision. Ya'qub read it with the *ya'* retained. The majority read *al-munsha'at* with a *fatha* on the *shin*; Hamza and Abu Bakr in one transmission from him read it with a *kasra* on the *shin*.

﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For that is so clear and manifest that its denial or refusal is impossible.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it sound, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾, that he said: "By calculation and by stations through which they travel."

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning ﴿And the earth He laid out for all creatures﴾, that he said: "For the people."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, that he said: "For the creation."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "Everything that has a soul."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿And the palm tree with its sheaths﴾, that he said: "The containers of the spathe."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿And grain with its husk, and fragrant plants﴾, that he said: "The husk (*tibn*)." And "the fragrant plants" (*al-rayhan*), he said: "The greenness of the crops."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "*Al-'asf*" is the leaves of the crop when they dry out, and "*al-rayhan*" is what the earth produces of the fragrant plants that are smelled.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also, that he said: "*Al-'asf*" is the crop when it first emerges as green shoots, and "*al-rayhan*" is when it stands firm on its stalk and has not yet formed an ear.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "Every *rayhan* in the Qur'an is provision (*rizq*)."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾, that he said: "That is, which of God's blessings."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "That is, the jinn and the humans."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him also concerning ﴿from a smokeless flame of fire﴾, that he said: "From the flame of fire."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "The pure part of the fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾, that he said: "The sun has a rising point in winter and a setting point in winter, and a rising point in summer and a setting point in summer, different from its rising point in winter and its setting point in winter."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning the verse, that he said: "The rising of the dawn and the rising of the twilight, and the setting of the sun and the setting of the twilight."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾, that he said: "He released the two seas. ﴿Between them is a barrier﴾," he said: "A partition. ﴿They do not transgress﴾, they do not mix."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from him also, that he said: "The sea of the sky and the sea of the earth."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning ﴿Between them is a barrier, they do not transgress﴾, that he said: "Between them is such a distance that neither one transgresses upon the other."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him also concerning His saying ﴿From them come forth pearls and coral﴾, that he said: "When the sky rains, the shells in the sea open their mouths, and whatever falls into them of the raindrops of the sky becomes pearl."

(p-1436) 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, that he said: "Coral is the large pearls."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Pearl is what is large of it, and coral is the small pearls."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "Coral is red beads."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 55, verses 1–25 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan.

Al-Qurtubi said: The whole surah is Meccan according to al-Hasan, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, 'Ikrima, 'Ata', and Jabir. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Except for one verse within it, which is His saying: ﴿He is asked by whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ (55:29)."

Ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said it is entirely Medinan. The first view is more sound, and it is supported by what al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'A'isha, who said: "The surah ﴿The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an﴾ (55:1–2) was revealed in Mecca."

Ahmad and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: with a *hasan* (good) chain, from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting while praying toward the Corner (of the Ka'ba), before he was commanded to proclaim openly, and the polytheists were listening: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾ (55:13)."

The second view is supported by what Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rahman was revealed in Medina." The two views can be reconciled by saying that part of it was revealed in Mecca and part in Medina.

al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama*, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out to his Companions and recited to them Surat al-Rahman from its beginning to its end, and they remained silent. He said: 'Why do I see you silent? I recited it to the jinn on the night of the jinn, and they gave a better response than you did. Every time I reached His saying: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord would you deny?﴾, they said: "None of Your blessings do we deny, our Lord, and to You belongs all praise."'"

al-Tirmidhi said after narrating it: "This is a *gharib* (strange) hadith, which we do not know except through the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad." [p. 1433]

It is related from Imam Ahmad that he used to disapprove of his narrating from Zuhayr.

al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it to be narrated except by this route."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Khatib in his *Tarikh* narrated it from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and al-Suyuti declared its chain sound.

al-Bazzar said: "We do not know it to be narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) except by this route with this chain."

al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* narrated from 'Ali, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Everything has a bride, and the bride of the Qur'an is al-Rahman.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

His saying ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾: The *raf'* (nominative case) of "al-Rahman" is because it is the *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and what follows it of verbs are its *akhbar* (predicates).

It may also be that it is the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'*, meaning: "He is Allah, the Most Merciful."

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of ﴿taught the Qur'an﴾ is "made it easy."

al-Kalbi said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ to Muhammad, and Muhammad taught it to his community. It was also said that He made it a sign of what He has made people worship by. It was said that this verse was revealed as a response to the people of Mecca when they said: "It is only a human who teaches him." It was also said it was a response to their saying: "And what is al-Rahman?"

Since this surah enumerates the favors which He has bestowed upon His servants, He began with the favor that is greatest in rank, most abundant in benefit, most complete in usefulness, and most far-reaching in its return, which is the favor of teaching the Qur'an, for it is the axis of the happiness of both abodes, the pivot of both goods, and the pillar of both matters.

Then, after this favor, He bestowed the favor of creation, which is the basis of all affairs and the return of all things, and so He said: ﴿He created man﴾ (55:3). Thirdly, He bestowed favor by teaching him *al-bayan* (clear expression), by which understanding occurs, on which mutual discourse turns, and upon which the interests of this life and the Hereafter depend, for it is impossible to make manifest what is in the hearts or to reveal what turns in the mind except by it.

Qatada and al-Hasan said: "The intended 'man' here is Muhammad (ﷺ), and by *al-bayan* is meant the lawful from the unlawful and guidance from misguidance." But this is far-fetched.

al-Dahhak said: *al-bayan* is good and evil.

al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is what benefits him from what harms him.

It was said: *al-bayan* is writing with the pen.

The better view is to take "man" as the species, and to take *al-bayan* as Allah teaching every people their language, which they speak.

﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning﴾ (55:5): That is, they run according to calculation and to stations which they do not exceed, and by this they indicate the number of months and years.

Qatada and Abu Malik said: They run by a reckoning in their stations; they do not exceed them nor deviate from them.

Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kaysan said: It means that by them times, terms, and deeds are reckoned.

Had there been no night and day, the sun and the moon, no one would know how to calculate, because the age would be entirely night or entirely day.

al-Dahhak said: The meaning of *bi-husban* is "by measure."

Mujahid said: *bi-husban* is like the *husban* of a millstone, meaning its axis upon which they both revolve.

al-Akhfash said: *al-husban* is the plural of *al-hisab* (reckoning), like *shuhub* and *shuhban*.

As for *al-husban* with a *damma*, it means punishment, as has passed in Surat al-Kahf.

﴿And the star and the tree prostrate﴾ (55:6): *al-najm* is the plant that has no stalk, and *al-shajar* is that which has a stalk.

The poet said:
"The wide plain has grown its thickets of low plants,
and by it the two tribes of Tamim and Wa'il have been completed."

And Zuhayr said:
"Crowned with the roots of the *najm*, which the south wind weaves
for the bright waters of its surface, its patterns."

The intended meaning of their prostration is their submission to Allah, Exalted, in the manner of the prostrating among the responsible beings.

al-Farra' said: Their prostration is that they face the sun when it rises, then incline with it when the shade recedes.

al-Zajjaj said: Their prostration is the turning of the shadow with them, as in His saying: ﴿whose shadows turn around﴾ (16:48).

al-Hasan and Mujahid said: The intended "star" is a star of the sky, and its prostration is its rising. Ibn Jarir preferred this view.

It was also said: its prostration is its setting. And the prostration of the tree is its allowing its fruit to be picked.

al-Nahhas said: The origin of *sujud* (prostration) is submission and compliance to Allah. This sentence and the one before it are two other predicates of *al-Rahman*, and the connecting pronoun is omitted in them because it is clear, as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him."

﴿And the heaven He raised﴾ (55:7): The majority read *al-sama'* in the accusative by *al-ishtighal* (the construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring to the noun, so the noun is put in the accusative).

Abu al-Simak read it in the nominative by *al-ibtida'* (inception of a nominal sentence). The meaning is that He made the heaven raised above the earth. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾: The intended "balance" is justice. That is: He set in the earth the justice which He commanded. Thus said Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others.

al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that He commanded us to do justice, and what indicates this is His saying: ﴿that you not transgress in the balance﴾ (55:8), that is, do not exceed justice.

al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: The intended meaning is the instrument of weighing, by which one reaches fairness and equity.

It was said the balance is the Qur'an, because in it is the explanation of what is needed. Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said this, but the first view is better.

Then, after informing the servants that He had set it for them, He commanded them to establish justice, so He said: ﴿And establish the weight with justice﴾ (55:9), that is, make your weighing upright with justice. It was also said the meaning is: establish the tongue of the balance with justice. It was also said the meaning is: He set the balance for the weighing of deeds in the Hereafter.

In His saying ﴿that you not transgress﴾, *an* is *masdariyya* (a verbal-noun particle), meaning "so that you do not transgress." And *la* is negating, meaning: He set the balance so that you do not transgress. It was also said it is *mufassira* (explanatory), because in "setting" there is the sense of "saying." Transgression is exceeding the limit. Whoever says the balance is justice says its transgression is injustice, and whoever says the balance is the instrument by which one weighs says its transgression is cheating.

﴿And do not make the balance deficient﴾ (55:9): that is, do not diminish it. He, glory be to Him, first commanded equality, then forbade transgression, which is exceeding the limit by excess, then forbade deficiency, which is loss and cheating.

The majority read *tukhsiru* with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *sin*, from *akhsara*. Bilal ibn Abi Burda, Aban ibn 'Uthman, and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with a *fatha* on the *ta'* and the *sin*, from *khasira*. Both are dialects: it is said *akhsartu al-mizan* and *khasartuhu* (I made the balance deficient).

Then, after He mentioned that He raised the heaven, He mentioned that He set the earth, so He said: ﴿And the earth He set down for the creatures﴾ (55:10), that is, He spread it upon the water for all creation that has life and spirit. There is no basis for restricting *al-anam* (the creatures) to humans and jinn.
