It was said: one of each pair is fresh and the other dry, neither of them being inferior to the other in excellence or goodness.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For in merely enumerating these blessings and describing them in this Mighty Book, there is encouragement to do good and warning against doing evil, which is not hidden from one who understands. That is a great blessing and a grand favour, so how much more so is enjoying it upon arriving at it.

﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade﴾. The accusative of muttaki'in (reclining) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of His words: ﴿and for whoever fears﴾. It is plural in agreement with the meaning of man (whoever). It was said its governing element is omitted, the implied meaning being: "they enjoy themselves reclining."

It was also said it is in the accusative as a term of praise. Furush is the plural of farsh (bed), and al-bata'in are what lies beneath the outer covers (al-zahair), and is the plural of bitana (lining).

Al-Zajjaj said: al-bata'in are what is toward the ground. Al-istabraq is what is thick of brocade (al-dibaj). If the linings are of istabraq, how are the outer covers? It was said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The linings are of istabraq, so what are the outer surfaces?" He said: "This is according to what God says about it: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾." It was said that He only mentioned the linings because no one on earth knew what was in the outer covers.

Al-Hasan said: its linings are of istabraq and its outer covers are of solid light.

Al-Hasan also said: al-bata'in are the zahair. Al-Farra' said this too, and said: the bitana may be the zihara and the zihara the bitana, since each of them may be the face. The Arabs say "this is the back of the sky" and "this is the belly of the sky," referring to its outer side that we see. Ibn Qutayba denied this and said it applies only to two equal faces.

﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand﴾. Wa jana (fruit) is the subject, and dani (near) is its predicate. Al-jana is what is picked from the fruits. It was said that the tree draws close until one who wishes to pick its fruit can pick it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"This is my picking, and its best is in it, since every picker brings his hand to his mouth."

The majority read furush with two damma-s, while Abu Hayawa read it with one damma and a sukun. The majority read jana with a fatha on the jim, while Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra. Isa also read the nun with a kasra as imala (vowel inclination).

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of these are in a place where it is not possible for a denier to deny any of them, because of the immediate and deferred benefits they include.

﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾, that is, in the two aforementioned gardens.

Al-Zajjaj said: He said "therein" (fihinna, feminine plural) because He meant the two gardens and the blessings prepared for their companions within them. It was also said: "therein" refers to the beds whose linings are of istabraq. The meaning of "restraining their gaze" is that they restrict their eyes to their husbands and do not look at others. This has already been explained in Surat al-Saffat.

﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-tamth is deflowering (al-iftida'), which is intercourse accompanied by bleeding. One says "tamatha the girl" when he takes her virginity.

Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: no one before them had touched them, had sexual relations with them, or had intercourse with them.

Muqatil said: because they were created in Paradise. The pronoun in "before them" refers to the husbands implied by "restraining their gaze." It was also said it refers to "reclining," and the clause is in the position of a nominative attribute of "restraining," since its annexation is merely verbal. It was also said that al-tamth means touching, that is, no one touched them. Abu 'Amr said this.

Al-Mubarrad said: that is, no one tamed them. Al-tamth means taming. Among the usages of tamth in the sense al-Farra' mentioned is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"They were delivered to me, untouched before me, and they are purer than ostrich eggs."

The majority read yatmithhunna with a kasra on the mim. Al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, and al-Jahdari and Talha ibn Musarrif read it with a fatha. In this verse, and indeed in many verses of this surah, there is evidence that the jinn enter Paradise if they believe in God, glory be to Him, and act upon His obligations and refrain from what He has forbidden.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For in merely this encouragement regarding these blessings there is a glorious blessing and a great favour, because through it arises eagerness for righteous deeds and flight from wicked deeds. So how much more so is arriving at these blessings and enjoying them in the gardens of bliss without cessation or end.

﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾. This is an attribute of "restraining their gaze," or a circumstantial state from them. God, glory be to Him, likened them in the purity of their color together with its redness to rubies and coral. Yaqut is the well-known stone, and marjan has already been discussed in this surah, with the disagreement over whether it is small pearls or the well-known red coral.

Al-Hasan said: they are in the clarity of rubies and the whiteness of coral. He specified coral according to the view that it is small pearls, because their clarity is greater than that of large pearls.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For none of His blessings can be denied, whatever they may be, so how much more so these great blessings and abundant bounties.

﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ This sentence confirms (p. 1440) what precedes it. The meaning is: what is the reward of one who did good deeds in this world but good treatment in the Hereafter? Ibn Zayd and others said so.

Ikrima said: "Is the reward of one who says 'There is no god but God' anything but Paradise?" Al-Sadiq said: "Is the reward of one to whom you have shown kindness from eternity anything but the preservation of kindness upon him forever?"

Al-Razi said: this verse has many aspects, to the point that it has been said there are three verses in the Qur'an, each of which carries a hundred interpretations: the first is His words: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾; the second is ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾; and the third is ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: it applies to both the righteous and the wicked: the righteous in the Hereafter, and the wicked in this world.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For among them is His kindness to you in this world and the Hereafter, through creation, provision, guidance to righteous deeds, and deterrence from deeds He does not approve.

﴿And below these two are two gardens﴾. That is, below those two gardens described with the aforementioned attributes are two other gardens for those who are below the people of the two earlier gardens among the people of Paradise. The meaning of "below them" is: in front of them and before them, that is, they are nearer to and closer to the Throne. It was said the first two gardens are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss, and the latter two are the Garden of Firdaws and the Garden of Refuge.

Ibn Jurayj said: there are four gardens: two of them are for the foremost, the drawn-near ones: ﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾ and two springs flowing. And two gardens are for the companions of the right: ﴿In both of them are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ and ﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾. Ibn Zayd said: the first two are of gold for the drawn-near ones, and the latter two are of silver for the companions of the right.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of them are truth and blessings that cannot be denied.

﴿Dark green﴾. This is the attribute, and what lies between them is parenthetical. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj said: from the greenness of both of them they have turned black from their lushness, and everything that has black on it from being well-watered is mudhamm (dark). Mujahid said: they are blackened. Al-duhma in the language is blackness. One says "a dark horse" (faras adham) and "a dark camel" (ba'ir adham) when their grayness intensifies until the whiteness within it disappears.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of them are manifest and clear blessings that cannot be denied or rejected.

﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾. Al-nadkh is the welling up of water from a spring. The meaning is that in the two aforementioned gardens are two spouting springs. The people of language said: al-nadkh with the dotted kha' is more common than al-nadh with the undotted ha'.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: they spray upon the friends of God with musk, ambergris and camphor in the homes of the people of Paradise, as the rain sprinkles.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they spray with all kinds of fruits and water.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For they are not a place for denial nor a place for rejection.

﴿In both of them are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates﴾. This is among the attributes of the two gardens mentioned shortly before. Although palm trees and pomegranates are part of the fruits, they are singled out for mention because of their excellent qualities and the abundance of their benefit compared to other fruits, as related by al-Zajjaj, al-Azhari and others. It was also said He singled them out because they are abundant in the land of the Arabs. It was said He singled them out because the palm is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is both fruit and medicine.

The majority of the scholars hold that they are among the fruits. Only Abu Hanifa disagreed, and his two companions, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, disagreed with him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 46–78 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ Among these favours are the blessings in the Gardens of Bliss, and merely relating them has an effect on the hearts of the listeners and draws them to obedience to the Lord of the worlds.

﴿Therein are good and beautiful [companions]﴾. The majority of reciters read ﴿khayrāt﴾ with a single letter ṭ (light pronunciation). Qatādah, Ibn al-Samayfa', Abū Rajā' al-‘Utāridī, Bakr ibn Ḥabīb al-Sahmī, Ibn Miqsam and al-Nahdī read it with the doubled letter (tashdīd). On the first reading it is the plural of khayrah, on the pattern fa‘lah with a sukūn on the ‘ayn, as in one says "a woman who is khayrah (good) and another who is sharrah (bad)"; or it is the plural of khayrah, a lightened form of khayyirah. On the second reading it is the plural of khayyirah with tashdīd.

Al-Wāḥidī said: The exegetes said: "al-khayrāt" are women of good character and beautiful faces.

It has been said that this attribute refers to the four gardens, but there is no basis for this, since the two first gardens have already been described as having women ﴿restraining their gaze﴾, ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾, and there is a vast difference between the two descriptions.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For none of them, whatever it may be, is open to denial.

﴿Húrun maqṣūrāt fī al-khiyām﴾ — ﴿Maidens, restrained within pavilions﴾. That is, confined. From it comes qaṣr (palace), because it confines whoever is in it. Ḥūr is the plural of ḥawrā’, who has intense whiteness of the eye and intense blackness of it. The explanation of the meaning of ḥawrā’ and the disagreement concerning it has already been mentioned.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿maqṣūrāt﴾ is that they are restricted to their husbands and do not desire anyone else; al-Wāḥidī related this from the exegetes.

The first meaning is preferable, and this is what Abū ‘Ubaydah, Muqātil and others said.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawharī) it is said: "qaṣartu al-shay' aqṣuruhu qaṣran" means "I confined it", and the meaning is that they are kept secluded in the pavilions.

Khiyām is the plural of khaymah, and it has been said it is also the plural of khiyam, and khiyam is the plural of khaymah. The khaymah is a frame of poles set up and shaded with cloth, so it is cooler than tents of hide. It has been said that a khaymah of the gardens' pavilions is a hollow pearl, a farsakh by a farsakh. The word ﴿ḥūrun﴾ is in the nominative as a substitute for ﴿khayrāt﴾.

﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾. Its explanation has already been given in the description of the two first gardens.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For all of them are blessings that cannot be disbelieved in, and bounties that cannot be denied.

﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾. The accusative of ﴿muttaki’īna﴾ is either as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or as a praise (madḥ), as has been mentioned before. Abū ‘Ubaydah said: al-rafārif are carpets (busut). This was also said by al-Ḥasan, Muqātil, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others.

Ibn ‘Uyaynah said: they are zarābī (rugs).

Ibn Kaysān said: they are cushions (marāfiq).

It is narrated from Abū ‘Ubaydah that he said: they are the border of a garment.

Al-Layth said: a kind of green garments. It has been said: raised couches, and it has been said: every wide garment.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-rafraf are green garments from which enclosures are made; the singular is rafrafah.

Al-Zajjāj said: They have said that al-rafraf here means the gardens' meadows. They have also said that al-rafraf are cushions, and they have said that al-rafraf are enclosures.

End of quotation from al-Ṣiḥāḥ.

Among those who said they are the meadows of the Garden was Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr. The derivation of rafraf is from rafa, yarifu, meaning "to rise", and from it comes rafrafat al-ṭā’ir, which is the moving of its wings in the air.

The majority read ﴿rafrafin﴾ in the singular. ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī read "rafārif" in the plural.

﴿And beautiful ‘abqarī [carpets]﴾. Al-‘Abqarī means zarābī (rugs) and embroidered tapestries (ṭanāfis al-mawshiyyah). Abū ‘Ubaydah said: every embroidered cloth of carpets is ‘abqarī, and it is attributed to a land where embroidery is made. Al-Farrā’ said: al-‘abqarī are the eight-piece tapestries; it has been said they are zarābī, it has been said carpets, and it has been said brocade.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: The origin of this is that ‘Abqar is a village inhabited by jinn, and to it is attributed everything superior. Al-Khalīl said: among the Arabs, al-‘abqarī is every noble, excellent, outstanding man or woman. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*With horses upon which is a ‘abqarī jinn, deserving one day to obtain and to rise above.*

Al-Jawharī said: al-‘Abqarī is a place which the Arabs claim is from the land of the jinn.

Labīd said:

*Elders and youths like the jinn of ‘Abqar.*

Then they attributed to it everything that they admired for its skill, excellence of craft and strength, and they said "‘abqarī". It is both singular and plural.

The majority read ﴿‘abqariyyin﴾. ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī read "‘abāqiriyy". It is also read "‘abāqir", and both are an attribution to ‘Abāqir, the name of a town. Quṭrub said: it is not an attributive form; it is like kursiyy and karāsiyy, and bukhtiyy and bakhātiyy.

The majority read ﴿khuḍrin﴾ with a ḍammah on the kh and a sukūn on the ḍ. It is also read with a ḍammah on both, and this is a rare dialect.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For each of them is too exalted to be subject to denial, and too great for a denier to deny it or a rejecter to reject it. We have already mentioned at the beginning of this surah the reason for the repetition of this verse, so we will not repeat it.

﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾. ‘Tabāraka’ is taf‘ala from al-barakah (blessing).

Al-Rāzī said: The origin of tabārak is from al-tabarruk, which is permanence and stability, and from it comes "barraka al-ba‘īr" (the camel knelt) and birkat al-mā’ (the water pool), because water is permanent. The meaning is: its name endures and is established, or goodness endures with Him, since barakah, although it derives from stability, is used for good. Or its meaning is: He is exalted and His status is raised.

It has also been said that its meaning is the glorification and sanctification of God, glory be to Him. If this blessing is attributed to His name, the Mighty and Majestic, then what do you think of His very essence, glory be to Him? It has been said that ism (name) here means attribute, and it has been said that it is superfluous, as in the saying of the poet:

*"By the year's end, then peace upon you both; whoever weeps for a full year has an excuse."*

The explanation of ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ has already been given in this surah.

The majority read ﴿dhī al-jalāl﴾ as an attribute of the Lord, glory be to Him. Ibn ‘Āmir read "dhū al-jalāl" as an attribute of "ism".

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, he said: God promised the believers who feared His standing and performed His obligations the Garden.

Ibn Jarīr also narrated from him concerning the verse: "He feared and then was mindful of God, and the one who fears is the one who undertakes obedience to God and abandons His disobedience."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓamah narrated from ‘Aṭā’ that it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated the same from Ibn Shawdhab.

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd concerning the verse that he said: "for whoever feared Him in this world."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, Ibn Manī‘, al-Ḥākim, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasā’ī, al-Bazzār, Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū al-Dardā’ that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse, ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. I said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals, O Messenger of God?" The Messenger of God ﷺ recited the second time, ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. I said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" He recited the third time, ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. I said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" He said: "Yes, even if the nose of Abū al-Dardā’ is rubbed in the dust."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Abū al-Dardā’ said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals, and even if the nose of Abū al-Dardā’ is rubbed in the dust."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Yasār, a client of the family of Mu‘āwiyah, from Abū al-Dardā’ concerning His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, that he said: It was said to Abū al-Dardā’: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" He said: "Whoever fears the standing before his Lord does not commit adultery and does not steal."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Shihāb who said: I was with Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik, and he said: Abū Hurayrah said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Abū Hurayrah said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" I said: That was only before the obligations were revealed; when the obligations were revealed, this ceased.

al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The gardens of Firdaws are four gardens: two gardens of gold, their adornments, buildings and what is in them; and two gardens of silver, their adornments, buildings and what is in them. Between the people and their gazing upon their Lord there will be nothing but the cloak of pride upon His face in the Garden of Eden."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Mūsā from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ and His saying ﴿And besides them are two gardens﴾, he said: "Two gardens of gold for those brought near, and two gardens of silver for the companions of the right."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from Abū Mūsā concerning His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, he said: "Two gardens of gold for the foremost, and two gardens of silver for the followers."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His saying ﴿Two gardens of branches﴾, he said: "Of various colours."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: "Its afnān (branches), its branches touch one another."

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: "The fann is the branch."

al-Firyābī, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in Zawā’id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd concerning His saying ﴿reclining on carpets whose linings are of brocade﴾, he said: "You are told of the linings, so how about the outer surfaces?"

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās that it was said to him: "Its linings are of brocade, so what are the outer surfaces?" He said: "That is among what God said: ﴿No soul knows what has been kept hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾."

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾, he said: "Its fruit (jannā) is its produce, and the near (dānī) is the one close to you, which can be reached by one standing or sitting."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from him also, concerning His saying: ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾, he said: "From other than their husbands. He did not touch them" means "He did not approach them" or "He did not deflower them."

Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His saying: ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾, he said: "She looks at her face within her curtain, purer than a mirror, and the least pearl upon her would illuminate what is between the east and the west. She wears seventy garments and his gaze penetrates them until he sees the marrow of her shin through all of that."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Hannād ibn al-Sarī, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in Ṣifat al-Jannah, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, Abū al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓamah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed a woman of the women of the people of the Garden, the whiteness of her shin is seen through seventy robes until its marrow is seen, because God says: ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾. As for the ruby, it is a stone which, if you insert a thread into it and then purify it, you would see it from behind it." al-Tirmidhī narrated it as a mawqūf (ending with a companion) report and said it is more authentic.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shu‘ab, who weakened it, narrated from Ibn ‘Umar who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said concerning His saying: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ "What is the reward of one whom you have blessed with monotheism except the Garden?"

al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl, al-Baghawī in his tafsir, al-Daylamī in Musnad al-Firdaws, and Ibn al-Najjār in his History narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet, the same as this.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jābir, traced to the Prophet, concerning the verse: "What is the reward of one whom We have blessed with Islam except that I admit him to the Garden?"

Ibn al-Najjār in his History narrated from ‘Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, traced to the Prophet, the same as the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 46–78 (part 3 of 3):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾" He said: Is the reward of one who says "There is no god but Allah" in this world anything but Paradise in the Hereafter?

Ibn Adi, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (and he declared it weak) narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah revealed this verse in Surat al-Rahman for the disbeliever and the Muslim: ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it as a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf).

Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "﴿Dark green﴾" He said: They are both green.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding the verse, He said: They have turned black from the greenness, from the abundance of water.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: "From Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿Dark green﴾, and he said: Both are green."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding "﴿Gushing﴾", He said: Overflowing.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, He said: They gush with water.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Jannah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: "﴿Good and beautiful [companions]﴾", He said: For every Muslim there is a tent of pearl (khayrah), and for every khayrah there is a tent, and for every tent there are four doors, through which Allah's gift, honour and present will come to him every day, which had not been before that. There will be no women who are overly cheerful, nor overly proud, nor bad-smelling, nor foul-mouthed; (they will be) fair maidens, as if they were a hidden pearl.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from another route from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (marfu').

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "﴿Maidens (hur)﴾", He said: white. "﴿Restrained (maqsurat)﴾", He said: confined within tents. He said: in tents of pearl.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated: "The hur are those with intensely black pupils."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The tents are hollow pearl."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The tent is a hollow pearl, its height in the sky is sixty miles; in each of its corners there are people for the believer whom others do not see; the believer goes around among them."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "﴿Reclining on green cushions (rafraf)﴾", He said: the surplus of the cushions, bedding and carpets.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: It is the surplus of the cushions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated through various routes from Ibn Abbas: "﴿Green cushions (rafraf khudr)﴾", He said: the cushions (mahabis). "﴿And beautiful rugs ('abqari hisan)﴾", He said: the zarabi (carpets).

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him regarding the verse, He said: The rafraf are gardens, and the 'abqari are the zarabi (carpets).

When He, glory be to Him, had finished enumerating the worldly blessings upon the two species (al-thaqalan, humankind and jinn), He mentioned the otherworldly blessings He had bestowed upon them, and said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. His "standing" (maqam) is the place where servants stand for reckoning, as in His words: ﴿the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. So maqam is a verbal noun meaning qiyam (standing). It was also said that the meaning is "fears the standing of his Lord over him," that is, His watching over his conditions and His knowledge of his deeds and words, as in His words: ﴿Is then He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned [like one who does not]?﴾ Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: this refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers God and abandons it out of fear of Him.

The commentators differed concerning the two gardens. Muqatil said: they are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss. It was also said: one is the garden created for him and the other is the one he inherits. It was said: one is his own dwelling and the other is the dwelling of his spouses. It was said: one is the lower mansions and the other is the higher ones. It was said: one garden is for the fearful human and one for the fearful jinn. It was said: one garden is for performing obedience and the other for abstaining from disobedience. It was said: one garden is for the creed he holds and the other for the deed he performs. It was said: one garden is by his works and the other by God's bounty. It was said: one garden is spiritual and the other physical. It was said: one garden is for his fear of his Lord and the other for his abandonment of his desire.

Al-Farra' said: they are in fact one garden, and the dual form is used to match the rhyme of the verses (ru'us al-ayy).

Al-Nahhas said: this view is among the greatest errors against the Book of God, for God says: ﴿two gardens﴾ and describes them by what follows concerning them, etc.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For this great blessing is among them: granting the one who fears the standing before his Lord two gardens endowed with noble and magnificent attributes.

﴿Both of them having branches﴾. This is an attribute of "the two gardens," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. Al-afnan (branches) are the boughs, singular fanan, which is the branch that grows straight in length. Mujahid, Ikrima, Atiyya and others said this.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-afnan are types (alwan), singular fann, which means a kind of every thing. 'Ata' said this as well. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said so. 'Ata' combined the two views and said: on every branch are varieties of fruit. The use of fanan to mean a branch appears in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"The call of a dove calling Hadil, grieving, upon a branch singing."

And in the verse of another poet:

"What has stirred your longing but the cooing of a dove calling, upon the branches of the boughs, the doves?"

It was also said that the meaning of ﴿having branches﴾ is "possessing abundance and superiority over whatever else there is." Qatada said this. It was also said: al-afnan means the shade of the branches cast upon the walls. This was reported from Mujahid and Ikrima.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For each one of them is not a place for denial nor an object for rejection.

﴿In both of them are two springs flowing﴾. This is also another attribute of "two gardens": that is, in each of them there is a flowing spring.

Al-Hasan said: one of them is Salsabil and the other is Tasnim.

'Atiyya said: one is of water unchanging, and the other is of wine, delicious to those who drink it. It was said: each of them is like the worldly life multiplied manifold.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For among them is this blessing existing in Paradise for the people of felicity.

﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾. This is a third attribute of "two gardens." The zawjan (pairs) are two kinds and two types. The meaning is that in the two gardens, of every type of fruit one enjoys, there are two varieties, each type of which is delightful. It was said: one of each pair is fresh and the other dry, neither of them being inferior to the other in excellence or goodness.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For in merely enumerating these blessings and describing them in this Mighty Book, there is encouragement to do good and warning against doing evil, which is not hidden from one who understands. That is a great blessing and a grand favour, so how much more so is enjoying it upon arriving at it.

﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade﴾. The accusative of muttaki'in (reclining) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of His words: ﴿and for whoever fears﴾. It is plural in agreement with the meaning of man (whoever). It was said its governing element is omitted, the implied meaning being: "they enjoy themselves reclining."

It was also said it is in the accusative as a term of praise. Furush is the plural of farsh (bed), and al-bata'in are what lies beneath the outer covers (al-zahair), and is the plural of bitana (lining).

Al-Zajjaj said: al-bata'in are what is toward the ground. Al-istabraq is what is thick of brocade (al-dibaj). If the linings are of istabraq, how are the outer covers? It was said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The linings are of istabraq, so what are the outer surfaces?" He said: "This is according to what God says about it: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾." It was said that He only mentioned the linings because no one on earth knew what was in the outer covers.

Al-Hasan said: its linings are of istabraq and its outer covers are of solid light.

Al-Hasan also said: al-bata'in are the zahair. Al-Farra' said this too, and said: the bitana may be the zihara and the zihara the bitana, since each of them may be the face. The Arabs say "this is the back of the sky" and "this is the belly of the sky," referring to its outer side that we see. Ibn Qutayba denied this and said it applies only to two equal faces.

﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand﴾. Wa jana (fruit) is the subject, and dani (near) is its predicate. Al-jana is what is picked from the fruits. It was said that the tree draws close until one who wishes to pick its fruit can pick it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"This is my picking, and its best is in it, since every picker brings his hand to his mouth."

The majority read furush with two damma-s, while Abu Hayawa read it with one damma and a sukun. The majority read jana with a fatha on the jim, while Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra. Isa also read the nun with a kasra as imala (vowel inclination).

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of these are in a place where it is not possible for a denier to deny any of them, because of the immediate and deferred benefits they include.

﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾, that is, in the two aforementioned gardens.

Al-Zajjaj said: He said "therein" (fihinna, feminine plural) because He meant the two gardens and the blessings prepared for their companions within them. It was also said: "therein" refers to the beds whose linings are of istabraq. The meaning of "restraining their gaze" is that they restrict their eyes to their husbands and do not look at others. This has already been explained in Surat al-Saffat.

﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-tamth is deflowering (al-iftida'), which is intercourse accompanied by bleeding. One says "tamatha the girl" when he takes her virginity.

Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: no one before them had touched them, had sexual relations with them, or had intercourse with them.

Muqatil said: because they were created in Paradise. The pronoun in "before them" refers to the husbands implied by "restraining their gaze." It was also said it refers to "reclining," and the clause is in the position of a nominative attribute of "restraining," since its annexation is merely verbal. It was also said that al-tamth means touching, that is, no one touched them. Abu 'Amr said this.

Al-Mubarrad said: that is, no one tamed them. Al-tamth means taming. Among the usages of tamth in the sense al-Farra' mentioned is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"They were delivered to me, untouched before me, and they are purer than ostrich eggs."

The majority read yatmithhunna with a kasra on the mim. Al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, and al-Jahdari and Talha ibn Musarrif read it with a fatha. In this verse, and indeed in many verses of this surah, there is evidence that the jinn enter Paradise if they believe in God, glory be to Him, and act upon His obligations and refrain from what He has forbidden.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For in merely this encouragement regarding these blessings there is a glorious blessing and a great favour, because through it arises eagerness for righteous deeds and flight from wicked deeds. So how much more so is arriving at these blessings and enjoying them in the gardens of bliss without cessation or end.

﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾. This is an attribute of "restraining their gaze," or a circumstantial state from them. God, glory be to Him, likened them in the purity of their color together with its redness to rubies and coral. Yaqut is the well-known stone, and marjan has already been discussed in this surah, with the disagreement over whether it is small pearls or the well-known red coral.

Al-Hasan said: they are in the clarity of rubies and the whiteness of coral. He specified coral according to the view that it is small pearls, because their clarity is greater than that of large pearls.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For none of His blessings can be denied, whatever they may be, so how much more so these great blessings and abundant bounties.

﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ This sentence confirms (p. 1440) what precedes it. The meaning is: what is the reward of one who did good deeds in this world but good treatment in the Hereafter? Ibn Zayd and others said so.

Ikrima said: "Is the reward of one who says 'There is no god but God' anything but Paradise?" Al-Sadiq said: "Is the reward of one to whom you have shown kindness from eternity anything but the preservation of kindness upon him forever?"

Al-Razi said: this verse has many aspects, to the point that it has been said there are three verses in the Qur'an, each of which carries a hundred interpretations: the first is His words: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾; the second is ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾; and the third is ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: it applies to both the righteous and the wicked: the righteous in the Hereafter, and the wicked in this world.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For among them is His kindness to you in this world and the Hereafter, through creation, provision, guidance to righteous deeds, and deterrence from deeds He does not approve.

﴿And below these two are two gardens﴾. That is, below those two gardens described with the aforementioned attributes are two other gardens for those who are below the people of the two earlier gardens among the people of Paradise. The meaning of "below them" is: in front of them and before them, that is, they are nearer to and closer to the Throne. It was said the first two gardens are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss, and the latter two are the Garden of Firdaws and the Garden of Refuge.

Ibn Jurayj said: there are four gardens: two of them are for the foremost, the drawn-near ones: ﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾ and two springs flowing. And two gardens are for the companions of the right: ﴿In both of them are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ and ﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾. Ibn Zayd said: the first two are of gold for the drawn-near ones, and the latter two are of silver for the companions of the right.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of them are truth and blessings that cannot be denied.

﴿Dark green﴾. This is the attribute, and what lies between them is parenthetical. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj said: from the greenness of both of them they have turned black from their lushness, and everything that has black on it from being well-watered is mudhamm (dark). Mujahid said: they are blackened. Al-duhma in the language is blackness. One says "a dark horse" (faras adham) and "a dark camel" (ba'ir adham) when their grayness intensifies until the whiteness within it disappears.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of them are manifest and clear blessings that cannot be denied or rejected.

﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾. Al-nadkh is the welling up of water from a spring. The meaning is that in the two aforementioned gardens are two spouting springs. The people of language said: al-nadkh with the dotted kha' is more common than al-nadh with the undotted ha'.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: they spray upon the friends of God with musk, ambergris and camphor in the homes of the people of Paradise, as the rain sprinkles.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they spray with all kinds of fruits and water.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For they are not a place for denial nor a place for rejection.

﴿In both of them are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates﴾. This is among the attributes of the two gardens mentioned shortly before. Although palm trees and pomegranates are part of the fruits, they are singled out for mention because of their excellent qualities and the abundance of their benefit compared to other fruits, as related by al-Zajjaj, al-Azhari and others. It was also said He singled them out because they are abundant in the land of the Arabs. It was said He singled them out because the palm is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is both fruit and medicine.

The majority of the scholars hold that they are among the fruits. Only Abu Hanifa disagreed, and his two companions, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, disagreed with him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 46–78 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ Among these favours are the blessings in the Gardens of Bliss, and merely relating them has an effect on the hearts of the listeners and draws them to obedience to the Lord of the worlds.

﴿Therein are good and beautiful [companions]﴾. The majority of reciters read ﴿khayrāt﴾ with a single letter ṭ (light pronunciation). Qatādah, Ibn al-Samayfa', Abū Rajā' al-‘Utāridī, Bakr ibn Ḥabīb al-Sahmī, Ibn Miqsam and al-Nahdī read it with the doubled letter (tashdīd). On the first reading it is the plural of khayrah, on the pattern fa‘lah with a sukūn on the ‘ayn, as in one says "a woman who is khayrah (good) and another who is sharrah (bad)"; or it is the plural of khayrah, a lightened form of khayyirah. On the second reading it is the plural of khayyirah with tashdīd.

Al-Wāḥidī said: The exegetes said: "al-khayrāt" are women of good character and beautiful faces.

It has been said that this attribute refers to the four gardens, but there is no basis for this, since the two first gardens have already been described as having women ﴿restraining their gaze﴾, ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾, and there is a vast difference between the two descriptions.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For none of them, whatever it may be, is open to denial.

﴿Húrun maqṣūrāt fī al-khiyām﴾ — ﴿Maidens, restrained within pavilions﴾. That is, confined. From it comes qaṣr (palace), because it confines whoever is in it. Ḥūr is the plural of ḥawrā’, who has intense whiteness of the eye and intense blackness of it. The explanation of the meaning of ḥawrā’ and the disagreement concerning it has already been mentioned.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿maqṣūrāt﴾ is that they are restricted to their husbands and do not desire anyone else; al-Wāḥidī related this from the exegetes.

The first meaning is preferable, and this is what Abū ‘Ubaydah, Muqātil and others said.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawharī) it is said: "qaṣartu al-shay' aqṣuruhu qaṣran" means "I confined it", and the meaning is that they are kept secluded in the pavilions.

Khiyām is the plural of khaymah, and it has been said it is also the plural of khiyam, and khiyam is the plural of khaymah. The khaymah is a frame of poles set up and shaded with cloth, so it is cooler than tents of hide. It has been said that a khaymah of the gardens' pavilions is a hollow pearl, a farsakh by a farsakh. The word ﴿ḥūrun﴾ is in the nominative as a substitute for ﴿khayrāt﴾.

﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾. Its explanation has already been given in the description of the two first gardens.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For all of them are blessings that cannot be disbelieved in, and bounties that cannot be denied.

﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾. The accusative of ﴿muttaki’īna﴾ is either as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or as a praise (madḥ), as has been mentioned before. Abū ‘Ubaydah said: al-rafārif are carpets (busut). This was also said by al-Ḥasan, Muqātil, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others.

Ibn ‘Uyaynah said: they are zarābī (rugs).

Ibn Kaysān said: they are cushions (marāfiq).

It is narrated from Abū ‘Ubaydah that he said: they are the border of a garment.

Al-Layth said: a kind of green garments. It has been said: raised couches, and it has been said: every wide garment.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-rafraf are green garments from which enclosures are made; the singular is rafrafah.

Al-Zajjāj said: They have said that al-rafraf here means the gardens' meadows. They have also said that al-rafraf are cushions, and they have said that al-rafraf are enclosures.

End of quotation from al-Ṣiḥāḥ.

Among those who said they are the meadows of the Garden was Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr. The derivation of rafraf is from rafa, yarifu, meaning "to rise", and from it comes rafrafat al-ṭā’ir, which is the moving of its wings in the air.

The majority read ﴿rafrafin﴾ in the singular. ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī read "rafārif" in the plural.

﴿And beautiful ‘abqarī [carpets]﴾. Al-‘Abqarī means zarābī (rugs) and embroidered tapestries (ṭanāfis al-mawshiyyah). Abū ‘Ubaydah said: every embroidered cloth of carpets is ‘abqarī, and it is attributed to a land where embroidery is made. Al-Farrā’ said: al-‘abqarī are the eight-piece tapestries; it has been said they are zarābī, it has been said carpets, and it has been said brocade.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: The origin of this is that ‘Abqar is a village inhabited by jinn, and to it is attributed everything superior. Al-Khalīl said: among the Arabs, al-‘abqarī is every noble, excellent, outstanding man or woman. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*With horses upon which is a ‘abqarī jinn, deserving one day to obtain and to rise above.*

Al-Jawharī said: al-‘Abqarī is a place which the Arabs claim is from the land of the jinn.

Labīd said:

*Elders and youths like the jinn of ‘Abqar.*

Then they attributed to it everything that they admired for its skill, excellence of craft and strength, and they said "‘abqarī". It is both singular and plural.

The majority read ﴿‘abqariyyin﴾. ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī read "‘abāqiriyy". It is also read "‘abāqir", and both are an attribution to ‘Abāqir, the name of a town. Quṭrub said: it is not an attributive form; it is like kursiyy and karāsiyy, and bukhtiyy and bakhātiyy.

The majority read ﴿khuḍrin﴾ with a ḍammah on the kh and a sukūn on the ḍ. It is also read with a ḍammah on both, and this is a rare dialect.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For each of them is too exalted to be subject to denial, and too great for a denier to deny it or a rejecter to reject it. We have already mentioned at the beginning of this surah the reason for the repetition of this verse, so we will not repeat it.

﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾. ‘Tabāraka’ is taf‘ala from al-barakah (blessing).

Al-Rāzī said: The origin of tabārak is from al-tabarruk, which is permanence and stability, and from it comes "barraka al-ba‘īr" (the camel knelt) and birkat al-mā’ (the water pool), because water is permanent. The meaning is: its name endures and is established, or goodness endures with Him, since barakah, although it derives from stability, is used for good. Or its meaning is: He is exalted and His status is raised.

It has also been said that its meaning is the glorification and sanctification of God, glory be to Him. If this blessing is attributed to His name, the Mighty and Majestic, then what do you think of His very essence, glory be to Him? It has been said that ism (name) here means attribute, and it has been said that it is superfluous, as in the saying of the poet:

*"By the year's end, then peace upon you both; whoever weeps for a full year has an excuse."*

The explanation of ﴿Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ has already been given in this surah.

The majority read ﴿dhī al-jalāl﴾ as an attribute of the Lord, glory be to Him. Ibn ‘Āmir read "dhū al-jalāl" as an attribute of "ism".

Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās regarding His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, he said: God promised the believers who feared His standing and performed His obligations the Garden.

Ibn Jarīr also narrated from him concerning the verse: "He feared and then was mindful of God, and the one who fears is the one who undertakes obedience to God and abandons His disobedience."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓamah narrated from ‘Aṭā’ that it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated the same from Ibn Shawdhab.

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd concerning the verse that he said: "for whoever feared Him in this world."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, Ibn Manī‘, al-Ḥākim, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasā’ī, al-Bazzār, Abū Ya‘lā, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū al-Dardā’ that the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse, ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. I said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals, O Messenger of God?" The Messenger of God ﷺ recited the second time, ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. I said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" He recited the third time, ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. I said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" He said: "Yes, even if the nose of Abū al-Dardā’ is rubbed in the dust."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Abū al-Dardā’ said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals, and even if the nose of Abū al-Dardā’ is rubbed in the dust."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Yasār, a client of the family of Mu‘āwiyah, from Abū al-Dardā’ concerning His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, that he said: It was said to Abū al-Dardā’: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" He said: "Whoever fears the standing before his Lord does not commit adultery and does not steal."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Shihāb who said: I was with Hishām ibn ‘Abd al-Malik, and he said: Abū Hurayrah said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. Abū Hurayrah said: "Even if he commits adultery and steals?" I said: That was only before the obligations were revealed; when the obligations were revealed, this ceased.

al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The gardens of Firdaws are four gardens: two gardens of gold, their adornments, buildings and what is in them; and two gardens of silver, their adornments, buildings and what is in them. Between the people and their gazing upon their Lord there will be nothing but the cloak of pride upon His face in the Garden of Eden."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abū Mūsā from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾ and His saying ﴿And besides them are two gardens﴾, he said: "Two gardens of gold for those brought near, and two gardens of silver for the companions of the right."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from Abū Mūsā concerning His saying ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾, he said: "Two gardens of gold for the foremost, and two gardens of silver for the followers."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās concerning His saying ﴿Two gardens of branches﴾, he said: "Of various colours."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: "Its afnān (branches), its branches touch one another."

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated from him, saying: "The fann is the branch."

al-Firyābī, ‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, ‘Abd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in Zawā’id al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd concerning His saying ﴿reclining on carpets whose linings are of brocade﴾, he said: "You are told of the linings, so how about the outer surfaces?"

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ‘Abbās that it was said to him: "Its linings are of brocade, so what are the outer surfaces?" He said: "That is among what God said: ﴿No soul knows what has been kept hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾."

‘Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾, he said: "Its fruit (jannā) is its produce, and the near (dānī) is the one close to you, which can be reached by one standing or sitting."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from him also, concerning His saying: ﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾, he said: "From other than their husbands. He did not touch them" means "He did not approach them" or "He did not deflower them."

Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Ba‘th narrated from Abū Sa‘īd al-Khudrī from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His saying: ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾, he said: "She looks at her face within her curtain, purer than a mirror, and the least pearl upon her would illuminate what is between the east and the west. She wears seventy garments and his gaze penetrates them until he sees the marrow of her shin through all of that."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Hannād ibn al-Sarī, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in Ṣifat al-Jannah, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Ḥibbān, Abū al-Shaykh in al-‘Aẓamah and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas‘ūd from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Indeed a woman of the women of the people of the Garden, the whiteness of her shin is seen through seventy robes until its marrow is seen, because God says: ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾. As for the ruby, it is a stone which, if you insert a thread into it and then purify it, you would see it from behind it." al-Tirmidhī narrated it as a mawqūf (ending with a companion) report and said it is more authentic.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in al-Shu‘ab, who weakened it, narrated from Ibn ‘Umar who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said concerning His saying: ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ "What is the reward of one whom you have blessed with monotheism except the Garden?"

al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in Nawādir al-Uṣūl, al-Baghawī in his tafsir, al-Daylamī in Musnad al-Firdaws, and Ibn al-Najjār in his History narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet, the same as this.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jābir, traced to the Prophet, concerning the verse: "What is the reward of one whom We have blessed with Islam except that I admit him to the Garden?"

Ibn al-Najjār in his History narrated from ‘Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, traced to the Prophet, the same as the hadith of Ibn ‘Umar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 46–78 (part 3 of 3):

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾" He said: Is the reward of one who says "There is no god but Allah" in this world anything but Paradise in the Hereafter?

Ibn Adi, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman (and he declared it weak) narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah revealed this verse in Surat al-Rahman for the disbeliever and the Muslim: ﴿Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it as a statement of Ibn Abbas (mawquf).

Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: "﴿Dark green﴾" He said: They are both green.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding the verse, He said: They have turned black from the greenness, from the abundance of water.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated: "From Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿Dark green﴾, and he said: Both are green."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding "﴿Gushing﴾", He said: Overflowing.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him, He said: They gush with water.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in Sifat al-Jannah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His words: "﴿Good and beautiful [companions]﴾", He said: For every Muslim there is a tent of pearl (khayrah), and for every khayrah there is a tent, and for every tent there are four doors, through which Allah's gift, honour and present will come to him every day, which had not been before that. There will be no women who are overly cheerful, nor overly proud, nor bad-smelling, nor foul-mouthed; (they will be) fair maidens, as if they were a hidden pearl.

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated it from another route from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (marfu').

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "﴿Maidens (hur)﴾", He said: white. "﴿Restrained (maqsurat)﴾", He said: confined within tents. He said: in tents of pearl.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated: "The hur are those with intensely black pupils."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The tents are hollow pearl."

al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The tent is a hollow pearl, its height in the sky is sixty miles; in each of its corners there are people for the believer whom others do not see; the believer goes around among them."

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding His words: "﴿Reclining on green cushions (rafraf)﴾", He said: the surplus of the cushions, bedding and carpets.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: It is the surplus of the cushions.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated through various routes from Ibn Abbas: "﴿Green cushions (rafraf khudr)﴾", He said: the cushions (mahabis). "﴿And beautiful rugs ('abqari hisan)﴾", He said: the zarabi (carpets).

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from him regarding the verse, He said: The rafraf are gardens, and the 'abqari are the zarabi (carpets).

When He, glory be to Him, had finished enumerating the worldly blessings upon the two species (al-thaqalan, humankind and jinn), He mentioned the otherworldly blessings He had bestowed upon them, and said: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens﴾. His "standing" (maqam) is the place where servants stand for reckoning, as in His words: ﴿the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6]. So maqam is a verbal noun meaning qiyam (standing). It was also said that the meaning is "fears the standing of his Lord over him," that is, His watching over his conditions and His knowledge of his deeds and words, as in His words: ﴿Is then He who is standing over every soul in what it has earned [like one who does not]?﴾ Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: this refers to a man who intends to commit a sin, then remembers God and abandons it out of fear of Him.

The commentators differed concerning the two gardens. Muqatil said: they are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss. It was also said: one is the garden created for him and the other is the one he inherits. It was said: one is his own dwelling and the other is the dwelling of his spouses. It was said: one is the lower mansions and the other is the higher ones. It was said: one garden is for the fearful human and one for the fearful jinn. It was said: one garden is for performing obedience and the other for abstaining from disobedience. It was said: one garden is for the creed he holds and the other for the deed he performs. It was said: one garden is by his works and the other by God's bounty. It was said: one garden is spiritual and the other physical. It was said: one garden is for his fear of his Lord and the other for his abandonment of his desire.

Al-Farra' said: they are in fact one garden, and the dual form is used to match the rhyme of the verses (ru'us al-ayy).

Al-Nahhas said: this view is among the greatest errors against the Book of God, for God says: ﴿two gardens﴾ and describes them by what follows concerning them, etc.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For this great blessing is among them: granting the one who fears the standing before his Lord two gardens endowed with noble and magnificent attributes.

﴿Both of them having branches﴾. This is an attribute of "the two gardens," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. Al-afnan (branches) are the boughs, singular fanan, which is the branch that grows straight in length. Mujahid, Ikrima, Atiyya and others said this.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-afnan are types (alwan), singular fann, which means a kind of every thing. 'Ata' said this as well. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said so. 'Ata' combined the two views and said: on every branch are varieties of fruit. The use of fanan to mean a branch appears in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"The call of a dove calling Hadil, grieving, upon a branch singing."

And in the verse of another poet:

"What has stirred your longing but the cooing of a dove calling, upon the branches of the boughs, the doves?"

It was also said that the meaning of ﴿having branches﴾ is "possessing abundance and superiority over whatever else there is." Qatada said this. It was also said: al-afnan means the shade of the branches cast upon the walls. This was reported from Mujahid and Ikrima.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For each one of them is not a place for denial nor an object for rejection.

﴿In both of them are two springs flowing﴾. This is also another attribute of "two gardens": that is, in each of them there is a flowing spring.

Al-Hasan said: one of them is Salsabil and the other is Tasnim.

'Atiyya said: one is of water unchanging, and the other is of wine, delicious to those who drink it. It was said: each of them is like the worldly life multiplied manifold.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For among them is this blessing existing in Paradise for the people of felicity.

﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾. This is a third attribute of "two gardens." The zawjan (pairs) are two kinds and two types. The meaning is that in the two gardens, of every type of fruit one enjoys, there are two varieties, each type of which is delightful. It was said: one of each pair is fresh and the other dry, neither of them being inferior to the other in excellence or goodness.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For in merely enumerating these blessings and describing them in this Mighty Book, there is encouragement to do good and warning against doing evil, which is not hidden from one who understands. That is a great blessing and a grand favour, so how much more so is enjoying it upon arriving at it.

﴿Reclining on beds whose linings are of brocade﴾. The accusative of muttaki'in (reclining) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the subject of His words: ﴿and for whoever fears﴾. It is plural in agreement with the meaning of man (whoever). It was said its governing element is omitted, the implied meaning being: "they enjoy themselves reclining."

It was also said it is in the accusative as a term of praise. Furush is the plural of farsh (bed), and al-bata'in are what lies beneath the outer covers (al-zahair), and is the plural of bitana (lining).

Al-Zajjaj said: al-bata'in are what is toward the ground. Al-istabraq is what is thick of brocade (al-dibaj). If the linings are of istabraq, how are the outer covers? It was said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The linings are of istabraq, so what are the outer surfaces?" He said: "This is according to what God says about it: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes﴾." It was said that He only mentioned the linings because no one on earth knew what was in the outer covers.

Al-Hasan said: its linings are of istabraq and its outer covers are of solid light.

Al-Hasan also said: al-bata'in are the zahair. Al-Farra' said this too, and said: the bitana may be the zihara and the zihara the bitana, since each of them may be the face. The Arabs say "this is the back of the sky" and "this is the belly of the sky," referring to its outer side that we see. Ibn Qutayba denied this and said it applies only to two equal faces.

﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand﴾. Wa jana (fruit) is the subject, and dani (near) is its predicate. Al-jana is what is picked from the fruits. It was said that the tree draws close until one who wishes to pick its fruit can pick it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"This is my picking, and its best is in it, since every picker brings his hand to his mouth."

The majority read furush with two damma-s, while Abu Hayawa read it with one damma and a sukun. The majority read jana with a fatha on the jim, while Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra. Isa also read the nun with a kasra as imala (vowel inclination).

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of these are in a place where it is not possible for a denier to deny any of them, because of the immediate and deferred benefits they include.

﴿Therein are those restraining their gaze﴾, that is, in the two aforementioned gardens.

Al-Zajjaj said: He said "therein" (fihinna, feminine plural) because He meant the two gardens and the blessings prepared for their companions within them. It was also said: "therein" refers to the beds whose linings are of istabraq. The meaning of "restraining their gaze" is that they restrict their eyes to their husbands and do not look at others. This has already been explained in Surat al-Saffat.

﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-tamth is deflowering (al-iftida'), which is intercourse accompanied by bleeding. One says "tamatha the girl" when he takes her virginity.

Al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: no one before them had touched them, had sexual relations with them, or had intercourse with them.

Muqatil said: because they were created in Paradise. The pronoun in "before them" refers to the husbands implied by "restraining their gaze." It was also said it refers to "reclining," and the clause is in the position of a nominative attribute of "restraining," since its annexation is merely verbal. It was also said that al-tamth means touching, that is, no one touched them. Abu 'Amr said this.

Al-Mubarrad said: that is, no one tamed them. Al-tamth means taming. Among the usages of tamth in the sense al-Farra' mentioned is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"They were delivered to me, untouched before me, and they are purer than ostrich eggs."

The majority read yatmithhunna with a kasra on the mim. Al-Kisa'i read it with a damma, and al-Jahdari and Talha ibn Musarrif read it with a fatha. In this verse, and indeed in many verses of this surah, there is evidence that the jinn enter Paradise if they believe in God, glory be to Him, and act upon His obligations and refrain from what He has forbidden.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For in merely this encouragement regarding these blessings there is a glorious blessing and a great favour, because through it arises eagerness for righteous deeds and flight from wicked deeds. So how much more so is arriving at these blessings and enjoying them in the gardens of bliss without cessation or end.

﴿As if they were rubies and coral﴾. This is an attribute of "restraining their gaze," or a circumstantial state from them. God, glory be to Him, likened them in the purity of their color together with its redness to rubies and coral. Yaqut is the well-known stone, and marjan has already been discussed in this surah, with the disagreement over whether it is small pearls or the well-known red coral.

Al-Hasan said: they are in the clarity of rubies and the whiteness of coral. He specified coral according to the view that it is small pearls, because their clarity is greater than that of large pearls.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For none of His blessings can be denied, whatever they may be, so how much more so these great blessings and abundant bounties.

﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾ This sentence confirms (p. 1440) what precedes it. The meaning is: what is the reward of one who did good deeds in this world but good treatment in the Hereafter? Ibn Zayd and others said so.

Ikrima said: "Is the reward of one who says 'There is no god but God' anything but Paradise?" Al-Sadiq said: "Is the reward of one to whom you have shown kindness from eternity anything but the preservation of kindness upon him forever?"

Al-Razi said: this verse has many aspects, to the point that it has been said there are three verses in the Qur'an, each of which carries a hundred interpretations: the first is His words: ﴿So remember Me, I will remember you﴾; the second is ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾; and the third is ﴿Is the reward of good anything but good?﴾

Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya said: it applies to both the righteous and the wicked: the righteous in the Hereafter, and the wicked in this world.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For among them is His kindness to you in this world and the Hereafter, through creation, provision, guidance to righteous deeds, and deterrence from deeds He does not approve.

﴿And below these two are two gardens﴾. That is, below those two gardens described with the aforementioned attributes are two other gardens for those who are below the people of the two earlier gardens among the people of Paradise. The meaning of "below them" is: in front of them and before them, that is, they are nearer to and closer to the Throne. It was said the first two gardens are the Garden of Eden and the Garden of Bliss, and the latter two are the Garden of Firdaws and the Garden of Refuge.

Ibn Jurayj said: there are four gardens: two of them are for the foremost, the drawn-near ones: ﴿In both of them is every fruit in pairs﴾ and two springs flowing. And two gardens are for the companions of the right: ﴿In both of them are fruit and palm trees and pomegranates﴾ and ﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾. Ibn Zayd said: the first two are of gold for the drawn-near ones, and the latter two are of silver for the companions of the right.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of them are truth and blessings that cannot be denied.

﴿Dark green﴾. This is the attribute, and what lies between them is parenthetical. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj said: from the greenness of both of them they have turned black from their lushness, and everything that has black on it from being well-watered is mudhamm (dark). Mujahid said: they are blackened. Al-duhma in the language is blackness. One says "a dark horse" (faras adham) and "a dark camel" (ba'ir adham) when their grayness intensifies until the whiteness within it disappears.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For all of them are manifest and clear blessings that cannot be denied or rejected.

﴿In both of them are two gushing springs﴾. Al-nadkh is the welling up of water from a spring. The meaning is that in the two aforementioned gardens are two spouting springs. The people of language said: al-nadkh with the dotted kha' is more common than al-nadh with the undotted ha'.

Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: they spray upon the friends of God with musk, ambergris and camphor in the homes of the people of Paradise, as the rain sprinkles.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they spray with all kinds of fruits and water.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord would you two deny?﴾ For they are not a place for denial nor a place for rejection.

﴿In both of them are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates﴾. This is among the attributes of the two gardens mentioned shortly before. Although palm trees and pomegranates are part of the fruits, they are singled out for mention because of their excellent qualities and the abundance of their benefit compared to other fruits, as related by al-Zajjaj, al-Azhari and others. It was also said He singled them out because they are abundant in the land of the Arabs. It was said He singled them out because the palm is both fruit and food, and the pomegranate is both fruit and medicine.

The majority of the scholars hold that they are among the fruits. Only Abu Hanifa disagreed, and his two companions, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, disagreed with him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 55, verses 46–78 (part 2 of 3):

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ Among these favours are the blessings in the Gardens of Bliss, and merely relating them has an effect on the hearts of the listeners and draws them to obedience to the Lord of the worlds.

﴿Therein are good and beautiful [companions]﴾. The majority of reciters read ﴿khayrāt﴾ with a single letter ṭ (light pronunciation). Qatādah, Ibn al-Samayfa', Abū Rajā' al-‘Utāridī, Bakr ibn Ḥabīb al-Sahmī, Ibn Miqsam and al-Nahdī read it with the doubled letter (tashdīd). On the first reading it is the plural of khayrah, on the pattern fa‘lah with a sukūn on the ‘ayn, as in one says "a woman who is khayrah (good) and another who is sharrah (bad)"; or it is the plural of khayrah, a lightened form of khayyirah. On the second reading it is the plural of khayyirah with tashdīd.

Al-Wāḥidī said: The exegetes said: "al-khayrāt" are women of good character and beautiful faces.

It has been said that this attribute refers to the four gardens, but there is no basis for this, since the two first gardens have already been described as having women ﴿restraining their gaze﴾, ﴿as if they were rubies and coral﴾, and there is a vast difference between the two descriptions.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For none of them, whatever it may be, is open to denial.

﴿Húrun maqṣūrāt fī al-khiyām﴾ — ﴿Maidens, restrained within pavilions﴾. That is, confined. From it comes qaṣr (palace), because it confines whoever is in it. Ḥūr is the plural of ḥawrā’, who has intense whiteness of the eye and intense blackness of it. The explanation of the meaning of ḥawrā’ and the disagreement concerning it has already been mentioned.

It has been said that the meaning of ﴿maqṣūrāt﴾ is that they are restricted to their husbands and do not desire anyone else; al-Wāḥidī related this from the exegetes.

The first meaning is preferable, and this is what Abū ‘Ubaydah, Muqātil and others said.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawharī) it is said: "qaṣartu al-shay' aqṣuruhu qaṣran" means "I confined it", and the meaning is that they are kept secluded in the pavilions.

Khiyām is the plural of khaymah, and it has been said it is also the plural of khiyam, and khiyam is the plural of khaymah. The khaymah is a frame of poles set up and shaded with cloth, so it is cooler than tents of hide. It has been said that a khaymah of the gardens' pavilions is a hollow pearl, a farsakh by a farsakh. The word ﴿ḥūrun﴾ is in the nominative as a substitute for ﴿khayrāt﴾.

﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them﴾. Its explanation has already been given in the description of the two first gardens.

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ For all of them are blessings that cannot be disbelieved in, and bounties that cannot be denied.

﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾. The accusative of ﴿muttaki’īna﴾ is either as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) or as a praise (madḥ), as has been mentioned before. Abū ‘Ubaydah said: al-rafārif are carpets (busut). This was also said by al-Ḥasan, Muqātil, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others.

Ibn ‘Uyaynah said: they are zarābī (rugs).

Ibn Kaysān said: they are cushions (marāfiq).

It is narrated from Abū ‘Ubaydah that he said: they are the border of a garment.

Al-Layth said: a kind of green garments. It has been said: raised couches, and it has been said: every wide garment.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-rafraf are green garments from which enclosures are made; the singular is rafrafah.

Al-Zajjāj said: They have said that al-rafraf here means the gardens' meadows. They have also said that al-rafraf are cushions, and they have said that al-rafraf are enclosures.

End of quotation from al-Ṣiḥāḥ.

Among those who said they are the meadows of the Garden was Sa‘īd ibn Jubayr. The derivation of rafraf is from rafa, yarifu, meaning "to rise", and from it comes rafrafat al-ṭā’ir, which is the moving of its wings in the air.

The majority read ﴿rafrafin﴾ in the singular. ‘Uthmān ibn ‘Affān, al-Ḥasan and al-Jaḥdarī read "rafārif" in the plural.

﴿And beautiful ‘abqarī [carpets]﴾. Al-‘Abqarī means zarābī (rugs) and embroidered tapestries (ṭanāfis al-mawshiyyah). Abū ‘Ubaydah said: every embroidered cloth of carpets is ‘abqarī, and it is attributed to a land where embroidery is made. Al-Farrā’ said: al-‘abqarī are the eight-piece tapestries; it has been said they are zarābī, it has been said carpets, and it has been said brocade.

Ibn al-Anbārī said: The origin of this is that ‘Abqar is a village inhabited by jinn, and to it is attributed everything superior. Al-Khalīl said: among the Arabs, al-‘abqarī is every noble, excellent, outstanding man or woman. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*With horses upon which is a ‘abqarī jinn, deserving one day to obtain and to rise above.*

Al-Jawharī said: al-‘Abqarī is a place which the Arabs claim is from the land of the jinn.

Labīd said:

*Elders and youths like the jinn of ‘Abqar.*
